**Surat al-Nisa'** (The Women)

Its central purpose is unity in monotheism (tawhid), to which Surat Ali 'Imran guided, and the Book, to which Surat al-Baqarah urged. This is for the sake of the religion, which Surat al-Fatihah gathered together, as a warning against what Sha's ibn Qays intended and what he schemed for, namely division.

This surah is among the last to be revealed. Al-Bukhari related in *Fada'il al-Qur'an*, from Yusuf ibn Mahak, that an Iraqi asked Umm al-Mu'minin 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, to show him her copy of the Mushaf. She said: "Why?" He said: "Perhaps I can arrange the Qur'an according to it, for it is recited out of order." She said: "What harm is it to you which you read first? What was first revealed of it was a surah from al-Mufassal (the shorter surahs), in which there is mention of Paradise and Hellfire. Then, when people turned to Islam, the lawful and the unlawful were revealed. Had the first thing revealed been, 'Do not drink wine,' they would have said, 'We will never abandon wine.' Had it been, 'Do not commit adultery,' they would have said, 'We will never abandon adultery.' Indeed, I was a young girl playing when Muhammad (ﷺ) received revelation at Makkah: ﴿Nay, the Hour is their appointed time, and the Hour is more calamitous and bitter﴾ [al-Qamar: 46]. And Surat al-Baqarah and Surat al-Nisa' were not revealed except while I was with him." He said: She then brought out the Mushaf for him and dictated to him the verses of the surahs. End of quotation.

By this, she, may Allah be pleased with her, meant that the Qur'an attained the highest eloquence (balaghah) in its revelation, being suited to what circumstances required according to the times. Then it was arranged in the highest forms of eloquence, according to what the meanings require of speech, as you witness in this wondrous Book, whose attainment is far. Since its purpose is unity upon what the two preceding surahs called to, of monotheism, and since the greatest cause of gathering and mutual connection is, customarily, the tender ties of kinship, which revolve around women, it was named "al-Nisa'" for this reason. Also, because through piety regarding them, chastity and justice are realized, whose essence is monotheism.

**In the name of Allah**, who gathers scattered affairs, by excellently arranging marriage among the subtle decrees; **the Most Merciful (al-Rahman)**, who made kinship a general mercy; **the Most Compassionate (al-Rahim)**, who specially favors whoever wills to maintain ties in accordance with what His religion calls to, which He made a complete blessing.

When the matter of the comprehensive Book, which is the Path, was established, and the supporting foundation, which is monotheism, was confirmed, the need arose for gathering upon that. So this surah came calling to gathering, connection, compassion, and mercy. It began with a general address to all people: ﴿O mankind﴾. This is because the mothers of virtues (ummahat al-fada'il), as explained in the science of ethics ('ilm al-akhlaq), are four: knowledge, courage, justice, and chastity, as their explanation will come in Surat Luqman, upon him be peace. Surat Ali 'Imran, along with what was mentioned of its purposes, called to two of them, namely knowledge and courage, as was indicated in more than one verse: ﴿He has sent down upon you the Book with truth﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 3]; ﴿And none knows its interpretation except Allah and those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 7]; ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him, and so do the angels and those of knowledge﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 18]; ﴿So do not weaken and do not grieve, for you will be superior if you are believers﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 139]; ﴿So they did not weaken for what afflicted them in the way of Allah﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 146]; ﴿And when you have decided, then rely upon Allah﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 159]; ﴿And never think of those who have been killed in the way of Allah as dead﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 169]; ﴿Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger after injury had struck them﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 172]; ﴿O you who have believed, be steadfast and endure﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 200]. And since the story of Uhud had resulted in orphans, whose inheritors had been martyred in the love of Allah, and since it was part of their practice in the Jahiliyyah to prevent such orphans from inheritance, out of injustice away from the right way and misguidance away from the straightest guidance, this surah came calling to the two remaining virtues, namely chastity and justice, along with emphasis on the two other traits as the context requires. This brings about connection through goodness and compassion through the correction of affairs, for gathering upon obedience to the Lord of Judgment. So its greatest purpose is gathering upon the religion by following the clear Book. How excellent is its beginning with the general, ﴿O mankind﴾, after the conclusion of the other with the specific, ﴿O you who have believed, be steadfast and endure﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 200], the verse!

Since this surah includes many kinds of obligations, among them showing compassion to the weak in matters they had been accustomed to opposing, which were extremely difficult for the souls, and since it indicated intense concern for them by opening and closing the surah with urging toward them, He said: ﴿Fear your Lord﴾, that is, your Master and Owner, who was good to you by nurturing you after bringing you into existence. Make between yourselves and His wrath a protection, lest He punish you by withdrawing His goodness toward you, and so bring down upon you every hardship. He began this by explaining (p-173) the manner of the beginning of creation, to build upon the foundation of piety, consisting of chastity and justice. He said: ﴿Who﴾ made between you the ultimate bond of kinship so that you would observe it and not waste it. That is because He ﴿created you from a single soul﴾, which is your father Adam, upon him be prayer and peace, reminding of His great power, as a warning to the disobedient and an encouragement to the obedient, as a preparation for the command concerning inheritance. He—glorified is He—made the command to piety the opening of two surahs: this one, which is the fourth of the first half, and al-Hajj, which is the fourth of the second half. He gave the reason for the command to piety in this one by what indicates the perfection of His power, the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, and the completeness of His wisdom regarding the matter of origin (mabda'). In al-Hajj He gave the reason for it by depicting the return (ma'ad) in a depiction beyond which there is no increase. So it indicated both origin and return, alerting that this is the locus of wisdom, for existence was not created except for its sake, so that the Most Beautiful Names and the Exalted Attributes might appear in the fullest manifestation humans can perceive. He arranged that in the most judicious order, placing the surah of origin before the surah of return, so that the recited verses would correspond to the visible signs.

More wondrous and precise than all of this: since the greatest purpose of the preceding surah was the dispute concerning 'Isa, and that his example is like the example of Adam, upon them both be prayer and peace; and since the reality of his condition was that he was a male born from a female alone, without an intermediary male (p-174), He clarified in this surah—by His saying, connected to what is implied, as an answer to one who seems to have asked: "How was that?"—"the creation of that soul" (or the sentence is in the circumstantial mode): ﴿and created from it its mate﴾, that is, his example in this respect is also like the example of Hawwa', his mother, for she is a female who was born from a male without an intermediary female. Thus his example became like that of each of his parents, Adam and Hawwa' together, upon them both be prayer and peace. The announcement of the creation of Adam, his spouse, and 'Isa, upon them all be prayer and peace, became included under the verse ﴿some of you from others﴾ [al-Nisa': 25], together with the verse of dispersal that follows this one, limiting the rational fourfold division which admits no increase: (1) a human not from a male nor a female; (2) a human from both of them; (3) a human from a male alone; (4) a human from a female alone. Therefore, in this surah He expressed by "creation" (khalq), and in other places He expressed by "making" (ja'l), because the context there is free of this purpose. This is supported by His saying—exalted is He—concerning the matter of Yahya, upon him be prayer and peace: ﴿Thus Allah does what He wills﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 40]; and concerning the matter of 'Isa, upon him be prayer and peace: ﴿He creates what He wills﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 47]. Moreover, the context here is for warning, which necessitates piety, so "creation," which is greater in manifesting power—because it is the invention of causes and the ordering of effects upon them—was more fitting than "making," which is the ordering of effects upon their causes, even if there is no invention. Glory be to the Mighty, the All-Knowing, the Great, the Wise!

When He mentioned the act of creation (insha'), He used the word "Lord" (Rabb), which derives from nurturing (tarbiyah). And since (p-175) the whole—indicated by His saying—connected to what is implied: "and He spread from Him for you toward her," was ﴿and dispersed from both of them﴾, meaning He scattered and spread offspring through procreation. Since what was dispersed before that was non-existence, and He is the One who brought it into existence from non-existence, He used the indefinite to convey this: ﴿men in great number and women﴾ from a single soul. The goodness of each of the people toward each of them is from the bonds of kinship. He described the men without the women, though the women are more numerous, as an indication that men have a degree over them, for they are stronger, more prominent, more excellent, and more apparent to the eye, because of their dispersal, while women have concealment and privacy.

Since He—glorified and exalted is He—had commanded at the beginning of the verse to fear Him, indicating that He is worthy of this from them because He is their Lord, He joined to that command another command, indicating that He deserves it in Himself, because He is the one who encompasses all perfection, free from every trace of deficiency. So He said: ﴿And fear Allah﴾, that is, generally, because of His encompassing attributes, just as you fear Him particularly because of His goodness and nurturing toward you. Beware of Him and be watchful of Him, lest you sever your kinship ties which He made a means for your nurturing.

Since the purpose of this surah is connection, He described His sacred self with what indicates that: He said: ﴿by whom you ask one another﴾, that is, some of you ask others, ﴿by Him﴾, for His noble and holy name is not invoked except for mercy, righteousness, and compassion (p-176). Then He increased the purpose's clarity, saying: ﴿and the wombs﴾, that is, and fear severing the wombs by which you ask one another, for you say: "I adjure you by Allah and by the kinship tie." He gave the reason for this command by warning them of the consequences of His seizing, since He is aware of their secret and their open conduct, together with His all-encompassing power. He said, emphasizing—because people's acts of abandoning piety and severing kinship are the acts of one who doubts that he is under the eye of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, that is, the One encompassing in knowledge and power, ﴿is over you﴾—and the preposition for elevation carries a form of threat—﴿an Observer﴾. Hamzah read "al-arham" (the wombs) in the genitive, as the thing sworn by, to magnify it and to strongly alert that they have forgotten Allah in fulfilling their rights—just as He swore by the star, the fig, and others. Both readings indicate that the connection of kinship has a great station with Allah, since He joined it with His name, whether as a conjunction, as the verse ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him﴾ [al-Isra': 23] and others explain, or as an oath. The Muslims agree that the maintenance of kinship ties is obligatory, and the most entitled to that maintenance is the child, and the first of maintaining him is to choose for him a lawful place (i.e., a lawful mother).

(p-177) When it became clear from this that He, glorified and exalted be He, magnifies the bond of kinship by placing it within the context of His mention, through His Greatest Name, as He does in similar manner in more than one verse; and since the surah before it had already mentioned the story of "Uhud," which uncovered orphans; then He mentioned, in His saying, ﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 185], that death is prescribed and every soul must arrive at it. It is thus known that orphans must necessarily exist at all times. So He called to chastity and justice toward them, because after the near of kin they are the most deserving of those regarding whom one should be mindful of God and fear His watchfulness over them. He said: ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾. That is, the weak ones who have been separated from their fathers. The root of "yatm" (orphanhood) is "al-infirad" (being alone). ﴿Their property﴾: that is, set it right by good management of it, so that you hand it over to them after they reach maturity, as will come. Or the giving may be literal, and the orphanhood is considered in terms of what they once were, or in terms of the linguistic meaning of the term, which is simply being alone. How wonderfully he has placed this after the general command of the fear of God, and specified it with the verse commanding kinship, concluded with the attribute of "al-Raqīb" (the All-Watchful)! For it is no secret that there is no motive for justice toward orphans except watchfulness, since they have no helper; and they may be kin.

When He commanded chastity in their property, He followed it with a condemnation of greed, which drives the heedless to abandon what is commanded. He said: ﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good﴾. That is, do not burden yourselves with taking things by way of substitution. ﴿The bad﴾: that is, from among the wickedness than which there is no greater wickedness, (p-178) because it destroys the purpose of a person and ruins all his affairs. ﴿For the good﴾: that is, what is every matter that leads to noble character, that preserves honor and raises a person's standing. Then, after this general prohibition, he drew attention to a specific kind of it, and said, expressing it through eating, which the Arabs used to censure when done excessively, even when it is lawful and good, so how much more when it is unlawful and from the property of a weak person while one is free of need for it: ﴿And do not devour their property﴾. That is, do not benefit from it in any manner of benefit, ﴿combining it with your own property﴾, out of greed, avarice, and love for increase of this world, whose ill omen you have known, and the failure it caused in "Āl ʿImrān." He expressed it with "ilā" (to), indicating that eating is implicitly included in the meaning of joining, alerting that whenever it is joined to the property of the guardian, he will eat from it and thus fall into the prohibition. Therefore he urged leaving it preserved in its own separate state. Then he gave the reason for this in His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is a great sin﴾: that is, the eating is a sin and a destruction, ﴿great﴾.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 4, verse 3 (part 1 of 2):**

(p. 179) Since (Exalted is He) had established the divine practice that reproduction must pass through marriage, with the exception of Adam, Eve, and Jesus, peace be upon them, and since [the guardians] had been commanded to act justly with the property of orphans, and they were in charge of the affairs of their orphans, and they sometimes married those girls under their guardianship, this warning might have deterred them from marrying because of their fear of falling short in (p. 179) some right of theirs. So (Exalted is He) followed it, as a conjunction to something implied, meaning: "If you are confident of your own ability to act justly, then marry them and have other dealings with them," with: ﴿And if you fear﴾. He expressed it with the particle of doubt, to urge scrupulousness (wara'). ﴿That you will not deal justly﴾, i.e., that you will not be equitable, ﴿with the orphans﴾, while you are confident of your own ability to be just with other than them: ﴿then marry﴾. Since women are deficient in intellect and religion, He expressed them with the particle used for non-rational beings, as an indication of gentleness toward them and forbearance with them, and so He said: ﴿what﴾. Since "marry" conveyed permission that implies lawfulness, He understood "good" (ṭayyib) as "pleasant" (ladhīdh), released from the earlier prohibition, so that the statement would be general, specified by what comes later in the verse on prohibited women, and would not be taken to mean "lawful," lest this, besides being repetitive, lead the statement to be ambiguous (mujmal), since the lawfulness had not previously been made known. Interpreting it as general but specified (ʿāmm makhṣūs) is preferable, because it is a proof (ḥujjah) in cases other than the specified exceptions, whereas the ambiguous has no probative force at all. This was stated by Imam al-Razi, and so He said (Exalted is He): ﴿good﴾, i.e., the restriction of the earlier prohibition was removed from it, and it became pleasant. He followed it with a necessary qualifier, saying: ﴿for you﴾, and He stated explicitly what was understood by implication, saying: ﴿from among women﴾, i.e., other than them: ﴿two, three, or four﴾, i.e., this permitted marriage being distributed in this manner: two and two, three and three, and four and four, for each one. This ruling is understood from the conjunction with "wa" (and). Had it been with "aw" (or), it would have conveyed marriage only in one of these three ways (p. 180), and would not have conveyed the choice that allows combining them in the manner of distribution. This is clear evidence that women outnumber men.

Al-Bukhari, in his Tafsir, related from ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr that he asked ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, about the statement of (Exalted is He): ﴿And if you fear that you will not deal justly with the orphans﴾. She said: "O son of my sister, this is the orphan girl who is in the custody of her guardian; he shares with her in his property, and her wealth and beauty appeal to him, so her guardian wants to marry her without being just in her dower, so that he would give her what others would give her. So they were forbidden to marry them unless they dealt justly with them and gave them the highest customary dower. They were then commanded to marry whatever women were good for them, other than them." ʿUrwah said: "ʿĀʾishah said: 'And the people sought a ruling from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ after this verse, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿And they ask you concerning women﴾ [al-Nisa': 127].'" ʿĀʾishah said: "And the statement of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in another verse: ﴿and you desire to marry them﴾ [al-Nisa': 127], is the desire of one of you to turn away from his orphan when she is little in property and beauty." She said: "So they were forbidden to marry those whose property and beauty they coveted among the orphan women, except with equity, because of their aversion to them when they were little in property and beauty." In another narration: (p. 181) "in marriage." Just as they leave them when they are averse to them, it is not permitted for them to marry them when they desire them, unless they deal justly with them and give them their full right in the dower. This address is to free men, not to slaves, because a slave does not independently marry whatever is good for him; rather, the permission of his master is required.

Since women are like orphans in weakness, He said, giving the reason for the permission to marry:

﴿And if you fear that you will not be equitable﴾, i.e., in plurality (al-jamʿ); ﴿then one﴾, i.e., then marry only one, because restricting oneself to one is closer to justice, since there is no other wife to whom a share must be given, so justice would be required between her and him. Since good companionship, which leads to justice, depends on self-effacement, and since slave women, because they are humbled by estrangement and lack of family, are closer to good companionship, He equated the number of them, without limit, with the single free woman, saying:

﴿Or what﴾, i.e., marry what: ﴿your right hands possess﴾, for there is no division among them. The mention of "what the right hands possess" also indicates that the address from its beginning is specific to free men. ﴿That﴾, i.e., marrying other than orphans, and limiting oneself to few free women, and restricting oneself to slave women: ﴿is nearer﴾, i.e., closer ﴿to avoiding injustice﴾, i.e., that you incline by oppression away from the course of equity, which is the upright balance; or that your dependents increase. As for the single wife, the matter is clear; and as for (p. 182) slave women, it is by withdrawal (ʿazl), by not needing a servant for oneself or for them, by selling whichever of them one wishes, and by directing them to earn a living; or that you be in need and thereby wrong some women, or consume the property of orphans. Each of these meanings returns to a necessary meaning of the root on which it is based. For the root ʿ-L-Ā, in all six of its permutations with waw, ʿ-L-W, ʿ-W-L, L-W-ʿ, L-ʿ-W, W-ʿ-L, W-L-ʿ, and with yā' in its two forms, L-Y-ʿ and ʿ-Y-L, revolves around elevation, and it necessarily implies increase and inclination. From elevation come: al-ʿulūw (height), al-waʿl (mountain goat), and al-walaʿ (eager desire). From inclination and increase come: al-ʿawl (excess, or inclination). The rest of the root, with yā' or waw, is either for removal or for one of these meanings, as will be explained. So ʿalā, yaʿlū means: he rose. Al-ʿāliyah means: an upright young woman, because she is higher than her peers who are crooked. Al-ʿāliyah also means: one of the districts of Hijaz, because of its overlooking what surrounds it. Likewise al-ʿawālī, the name of villages on the outskirts of the noble city of Madinah, because they are in a high place from which water flows to other places. Al-maʿlāh means: the acquisition of honor, and the cemetery of Makkah at al-Ḥajūn, because it is at the highest part of Makkah, and its water flows downward. "Fulān is among the ʿiliyyat of the people" means: among their nobles. Al-ʿilliyyah, with shaddah, means: the upper room, and "upon" (ʿalā) is the particle of elevation. "The woman became ʿallat from her postnatal bleeding" means: she became pure and recovered, because she had been in a state of lowliness. Al-ʿilāwah means: the top of a mountain and its neck, and what is loaded on a camel between its two packs; and from everything, that which exceeds it. Al-muʿallā means: the seventh arrow of the game of chance (maysir), because it is the goal among the winning arrows, since the arrows are ten; the first seven of them are winners, and the last three are unused and have no shares. ʿUlwān al-kitāb means: its title, and its elevation over the rest of the book is clear. Al-ʿiliyyān means: the tall, the large, and the high-standing she-camel; and among sounds, the loud. Al-ʿalāh means: the anvil. Al-ʿalyāʾ means: the top of every towering mountain, and the sky, and the high place, and everything that is high of anything. ʿAlayka Zaydan means: hold fast to Zayd, because by holding fast to him one attains superiority over his affair. ʿalā al-nahār means: the day rose. ʿalā al-dābbah means: he mounted the beast. Aʿlā ʿanhā means: he descended, as if it were from removal. Likewise ʿallā al-matāʿ ʿan al-dābbah, taʿlīyah, means: he lowered the goods from the beast. Aʿlaytu ʿan al-wisādah means: I removed myself from the pillow. ʿAlāytu means: I rose and withdrew. Rajulun ʿāli al-kaʿb means: a noble man. ʿAllā al-kitāb, taʿlīyah, means: he titled the book, like ʿalwanahu. ʿAlawū naʿyahu means: they publicized his death. Al-ʿAlī means: the strong and mighty. ʿIlliyyūn means: in the seventh heaven. (p. 184) Akhadhahu ʿulūwan means: he seized it by force. Al-taʿālī means: elevation. When you command from it you say: taʿāl, with a fatḥah on the lām; and to a woman: taʿālī, with a fatḥah on the lām. Even if you are in a place lower than the place of the one commanded, because it requires raising oneself up, however far the distance between you and him; and because the commander is higher than the commanded in rank, so his place is likewise. Taʿallā means: he rose gradually. Al-muʿtalī means: the lion. Al-lawʿ means: the one of bad character, the cowardly, and the greedy. Al-lāʿī means: the one whom the slightest thing frightens; either because he has reached the extreme of lowliness, so he climbed to its summit, until he accepted these traits for himself; or because it is from the category of removal, or of naming by the opposite. Dhi'bah laʿwah and imra'ah laʿwah mean: greedy she-wolf and greedy woman. Al-laʿwah means: the blackness between the two nipples of the breast, either because that is its highest point, or because the blackness is higher than the color of the breast. Al-alʿāʾ means: the phalanges, and the salāmā, a bone in the hoof of a camel; and small bones in the hand and the foot. This is because the bones are the highest of what is in the body in strength, firmness, and hardness, and they are its greatest support. Al-lāʿiyah means: a small tree on the slope of a mountain, which has yellow flowers and has milk; and if something of it is thrown into a pool of fish, it causes them to float, that is, to rise to the surface of the water. It was named so either from removal, in view of the place of its dwelling; or because its smell rises above everything it mixes with and imparts its taste to it; or because of its effect on fish. Talaʿʿā al-ʿasal means: the honey thickened in weight and meaning, either from al-lāʿiyah, because it is abundant in knots, or from the necessary consequence of height: strength and firmness. Laʿā laka, said at a stumble, means: may Allah lift you up. Al-ʿawl means: the rising of the reckoning in the inheritance shares. Al-ʿawl also means: inclination, and it was previously stated that it is necessarily associated with height. Al-ʿawl also means: every matter that overcame you, as if it rose above you so that you could not attain it; and the one sought for help, because nothing is reached through it except that there is elevation in it; and the provision of dependents, because it is the cause of their elevation. ʿAwwala ʿalayhi, muʿawwalan, means: he relied and depended. The noun is like ʿinab, and ʿayyil is like kayyis. ʿĀla means: he oppressed; and in the balance: it decreased or increased. The increase is from elevation, and the decrease is a necessary consequence of inclination. ʿĀlat al-farīḍah means: it rose, that is, its shares increased, so shortfall entered upon the heirs of the shares. Abū ʿUbayd said: I think it is derived from inclination. ʿĀla amruhum means: it intensified and grew severe. ʿĀla fulān ʿawlan wa ʿiyālan means: his dependents increased, like aʿwala and aʿyala. Rajulun muʿayyilun and muʿayyalun means: one with dependents. Aʿāla al-rajulu and aʿwala means: when he was greedy, either from what has been previously traced, or because it is necessarily associated with one who has dependents. ʿĀla ʿalayhi means: he carried, that is, he raised loads upon him, like ʿawala. Fulān means: he was greedy. Al-faras means: it neighed. Aʿwalat al-mar'ah means: the woman raised her voice in weeping. ʿĪla awluhu means: his mother was bereaved, because of the wailing that occurs from her cries. ʿĪla mā huwa ʿāʾiluhu means: what overcame the one who overcomes him was overcome; it is said of one whose speech or the like is admired, because no one is like this unless he has risen above his peers in elevation; and it may also be in lowliness, so it is from naming by the opposite. Al-ʿālah means: the ostrich, because it is the tallest of birds. Mā lahu ʿālun wa lā mālun means: nothing; because that is the extreme of lowliness if it is by incapacity, and of elevation if it is by asceticism. The one who stumbles is told: ʿālaka ʿāliyan, like the saying laʿā laka. Al-miʿwal means: an iron tool with which mountains are quarried, from the strength necessary for elevation. Al-ʿālah, like a canopy, by which one is shielded (p. 187) from the rain. Al-lawʿah means: a burning heat found from sorrow, or love, or sickness, or worry, because it rises over a person. Lāʿahu al-ḥubb means: love made him ill. Atānun lāʿat al-fuʾād ilā jaḥshihā means: as if she were distracted with fear for her foal. Lāʿa, yalāʿu means: he became distressed or sick. Rajulun hāʿun lāʿun means: a coward, distressed, or greedy, or of bad character, because these traits that are contrary to reason have risen over him and overpowered him. Lāʿathu al-shams means: the sun changed his color. Al-lāʿah also means: the iron-hearted, brave one, because he rises in dust. Imra'ah lāʿah means: a woman who flirts with you but does not allow you to have her, because of her overpowering and dominance over hearts. Al-waʿl means: the male mountain goat; and the noble; and the refuge. Al-waʿlah means: an inaccessible place on a mountain, or a rock overlooking it from it. Hum ʿalaynā waʿlun wāḥid means: they are gathered together. Mā laka ʿan dhālika waʿlun means: there is no escape from it; for if it were not for its height over you, you would not have been compelled to it. Al-waʿl (the text ends here)

(p. 188) **Shawwal** (the name of the month), as if it were so named because of its elevation by the ʿĪd and the Ḥajj; **al-waʿil** (the mountain goat), on the pattern of **kataf**: (the name of the month) **Shaʿbān**, because of its elevation, being situated between Rajab and Shawwal; **al-waʿla** also means:

the loop of a shirt collar; the **zīr** (button) and its **zirr**; the cup (qadaḥ); and the ewer (ibrīq) that is hung by it so that it rises above. **Waʿāl**, on the pattern of **ghurāb**: a fortress in Yemen. **Al-mustawʿal**, with a fatḥa on the ʿayn: the protected place of the mountain goat. **Waʿala**, on the pattern of **waʿada**: he rose high. **Tawaʿʿaltu al-jabal**: I ascended the mountain. **ʿAlawtuhu**: I climbed it. **Awlaʿa fulānun bi-kadhā**, or **walia** (with kasra): someone became fixated on such-and-such. **Istakhaffa**, meaning: he became elevated over it, overcoming it, because of his capacity to carry it. **Waliʿa bi-ḥaqqihi**: he went away (or departed with his right). **Wala'a** (with fatḥa): he lied, either for the sake of removal (of the truth), or because falsehood made him light and carried him away. **Walʿun wāliʿun**, as an intensive: a great lie. **Al-mūlaʿ**: the one in which there is a sheen of various colours, as if the colours are above it, or as if the basic colour of its hide overcomes those colours. The wording of the Qāmūs is: **al-tawlīʿ** is the lengthening of the piebald markings; it is said: "a horse (birdhawn) and a bull that is mūlaʿ," on the pattern of **muʿaẓẓam**. **Al-walīʿ**: the spathe of the date-palm flower while it is still in its sheath, that is, its covering (wiʿāʾ), which is the husk of the spathe, because of its height. **Mā adrī mā walaʿahu** (with fatḥa): I do not know what detained him; either for the sake of removal, because when he prevented him it was as though he removed his elevation; or because he rose over him and made him addicted to it, that is, incited him, that is, drove him to it. **Al-ʿaylah**: need; **ʿāla yaʿīlu**, when he became poor. This is either from removal, or because need overcame him, or because it is an inclination (mayl). **ʿĀlanī al-shayʾ**: the thing overpowered me. **ʿĪla ṣabrī**: my patience became scant and weak, that is, something of the matter overcame him, weakening him. **ʿIltu al-ḍāllah**: I did not know where to seek the lost animal. **Al-muʿīl**: (p. 189) the lion, the panther, and the wolf, because it seeks prey, that is, it searches; it returns to elevation and to the capacity to pursue. **ʿĀlanī al-shayʾ**: it made me destitute. Either it removed my elevation, or it rose above me. **ʿĀla fī mashyihi**: he swayed, strutted, and swaggered, because only one who is elated within himself does this, although all of it is from inclination (mayl). **ʿĀla fī al-arḍ**: he went off; that is, he rose over the earth by walking. The male hyena is called **ʿayalān**. **Al-ʿayal**, with the vowels moved: presenting your speech and words to one who does not want them and who is not concerned with them, as though he has not been guided to the one who wants them, so you present them to one who does not want them. This returns to the need that removes elevation. **Laywat al-jūʿ** (with fatḥa): its burning, as previously mentioned under **al-lawʿa**. **Liʿtu** (with kasra): I became weary, as if it were from removal, or because elevation belongs to the matter one is weary of. **Al-milyāʿ** (with kasra): the one quick to thirst, because she rises above the camels at that time, going ahead to the water, since thirst overcame her. **Al-milyāʿ**: the one who precedes the camels in advance, then returns to them. **Rīḥ liyāʿ** (with kasra): a strong wind.

With this, the correctness of what our Imam al-Shāfiʿī explained becomes clear, both explicitly and by correspondence, as previously mentioned. The usage **"al-awl fī al-ḥisāb wa al-sihām"** (the excess in the reckoning and in the arrows), meaning their multiplicity, bears witness to it. And the bias of those who rejected this became evident, when they said: it is not said of the multiplicity of dependants except "ʿāla yaʿīlu." How many a correct statement is criticised!

And how could it not be so? He is one of the imams whose statements in lexicography are relied upon, and others agreed with him, and the authentic hadith bears witness to his view.

Imam Yaḥyā ibn Abī al-Khayr al-ʿImrānī al-Shāfiʿī said in his book **al-Bayān**: regarding ﴿that you may not be unjust﴾, al-Shāfiʿī said: its meaning is: that your dependants (ʿiyāl) and those whom you support should not increase. It has also been said: most of the early generations (salaf) said: the meaning is: that you not be unjust. It is said: "ʿāla yaʿūlu" when he is unjust, and "aʿāla yuʿīlu" when his dependants increase. Except Zayd ibn Aslam, for he said: its meaning is that your dependants should not multiply. The statement of the Prophet (ﷺ) bears witness to this; he said: «Begin with yourself, then with those you support» (ibdaʾ bi-nafsika, thumma bi-man taʿūl). The end of the quotation.

This hadith was narrated by the two Shaykhs and others, from Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām, from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with them both), with the wording: «The best charity is that which is given out of surplus wealth; the upper hand is better than the lower hand; and begin with those you support.» Also on this topic there are reports from ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn, Abū Ramthah al-Balawī, and Abū Umāmah (may Allah be pleased with them all). The report of Zayd ibn Aslam was narrated by al-Dāraquṭnī and al-Bayhaqī through Saʿīd ibn Abī Hilāl, from him, who said: "That is nearer to ensuring that those they support do not increase." This was reported by our shaykh Ibn Ḥajar in his takhrīj of the hadiths of al-Rāfiʿī (p. 191).

The Imam said: the explanation of al-Shāfiʿī is the explanation of the community (al-jamāʿah); he expressed it by way of kināyah (allusion), which is mention of multiplicity, while meaning inclination, because multiplicity does not separate from it.

Ibn al-Zubayr said: When Sūrat al-Baqarah contained the beginning of creation and the bringing into existence of Ādam (peace be upon him) without a father or a mother, and it was followed by Sūrat Āl ʿImrān, because it contains, together with a mention at its beginning, the matter of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him), and that he is like Ādam (peace be upon him) in not needing a father; and those who are certain knew from this that, had He (exalted is He) willed, it would have been a sunnah for those after Ādam (peace be upon him), so that all other animals would depend only upon a mother; He (glorified is He) made known that whoever other than the two mentioned (peace be upon them both) among the descendants of Ādam, their way is the way of the two parents. So He (exalted is He) said: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 1], up to His saying: ﴿and He spread from them both many men and women﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 1]. Then He (exalted is He) made known the manner of marriage, which was made a cause of procreation, and what is connected with it, and He clarified the ruling on wombs and inheritances. So the sūrah contained the beginning of the matter and its end. He informed us of the manner of marriage, the form of mutual protection, the mutual respect among us, and how reconciliation is to be pursued between spouses when they quarrel and are in discord; and He made clear to us what may be married, and what number is permitted, and the ruling for one who does not find the means, and what is connected with this, up to inheritances. He detailed all of that, except divorce, because its rulings had already preceded; and because the foundation of this sūrah is upon connection, harmony, and observing the rights of kin, and preserving all of that until the state of death which is decreed upon us. The purpose of connection and affection is suited by what the sūrah opened with, His saying (exalted is He): ﴿He who created you from a single soul﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 1]. So it opened with unity and bonding. For this reason, from the ruling on the discord of spouses it was specified with informing of the form of reconciliation and fairness, to preserve that connection; so divorce was not suited to this, and no mention of it occurred here except by allusion: ﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 130]. And because of the great frequency with which the desires of the self arise, in marriage and with kinship, and this is subtle and obscure, the command to be mindful of God is repeated often in this sūrah, and with it the sūrah opens: ﴿Fear your Lord﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 1]; ﴿and fear Allah, through whom you ask one another, and the wombs﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 1]; ﴿And We had certainly enjoined those who were given the Scripture before you and yourselves to fear Allah﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 131]. Then they were warned against the state of one who persisted in disbelief, and the state of the Jews, the Christians, and the hypocrites, and of those who vacillate in religions after the certainty had come. All of that is emphasis on what they were commanded regarding mindfulness. The verses concluded (p. 193) with the matter of **al-kalālah** from the inheritances mentioned earlier. The end of the quotation.

When they were warned against the statement whose implication is an argument for having many wives, it was possible that someone would use it as a pretext to withhold some of the rights due, especially the bridal gift (ṣadāq) that he would make excessive. So He followed it with what negates that. He said, addressing the husbands, because the context concerns them, and expressing it in a way suited to repelling such a thought and to the commitment that prepares for it: ﴿And give the women their bridal gifts﴾, that is, generally, from orphans and others. ﴿Their bridal gifts﴾. His saying, emphasizing the giving with a verbal noun of similar meaning: ﴿as a gift (niḥlah)﴾, supports this, because its meaning is a gift given out of good will. Imam Abu 'Abd Allah al-Qazzaz said in his Diwan: Its root, that is, of "nahl" (gift), is the giving of a thing without seeking a return. And likewise, if we say the meaning of "niḥlah" is religion (diyānah), a creed (milla), a law (shir'ah), and a way (madhhab), that is, give them that as a matter of religion.

When this command was issued, it was possible that one who has taken on the character of Islam would refuse to accept what the woman willingly gives him of it by release or return, by way of a gift, thinking that this is not permissible, or for some other reason. So He said: ﴿But if they give you willingly﴾, that is, out of their own goodwill, ﴿of anything﴾. He made the pronoun singular so that it refers back to the bridal gift understood from "ṣadaqāt," and He did not say "of them" (minhā), lest it be thought that what is given is permissible only if it is the full bridal gift. So He said: ﴿of it﴾, that is, of the bridal gift, ﴿willingly﴾, that is, out of genuine desire, without compulsion (p-194) or deception. ﴿Then consume it﴾, that is, deal with it in every manner that is proper to you, ﴿with enjoyment (hanī'an)﴾, that is, agreeable, wholesome, pleasant, in well-being, without hardship or harm, ﴿with satisfaction (marī'an)﴾, that is, of good outcome, pleasing, delightful, with nothing troubling in it. Perhaps the partial expression (min shay'in) is a recommendation to abstain from accepting all of it, because in most cases that comes only from deception or vexation, and so it may be followed by regret. This statement also indicates the restriction to free persons, not slaves, since they do not own what women have given them to consume with enjoyment. Al-Asfahani said: If she has given it to him and then asks him for it back after the gift, it is known that her soul did not willingly give it. It is related from al-Sha'bi that a man came with his wife to Shurayh regarding a gift she had given him, and she was asking to take it back. Shurayh said: Return it to her. The man said: Did not God (exalted is He) say: ﴿But if they give you willingly﴾? He said: If her soul had been willing, she would not have taken it back. And from him (Shurayh) it is related that he said: I rule for her against what she gave, and I do not rule for him, because women deceive.

(p-195) When He commanded that the wealth of orphans, and of women, be handed over to them, and forbade consuming any part of it, He did so to make wealth seem less important and to show it little regard. Among the women and among the orphans under guardianship (*mahajir*, sing. *mahjur*, those placed under legal restraint) and others there were foolish persons. He commanded moderation in livelihood, out of caution against wronging others and against want, and He forbade extravagance (*tabdhir*). Glorified is He, who urged the good management of wealth in more than one verse of His Book, because "wealth is excellent for the righteous man who is righteous." This was narrated by Ahmad and Ibn Mani' from Amr ibn al-As, traced back to the Prophet. A person who does not have a free mind cannot carry out the pursuits of this world that concern him, and whoever cannot attain what concerns him of this world cannot attend to the affairs of the Hereafter. A person cannot have a free mind except through that which suffices him of wealth, because in this abode, which is founded on means, he cannot bring about benefits or ward off harms without it. Whoever seeks it for this purpose is among the greatest means that help him attain the happiness of the Hereafter, and whoever seeks it for himself is among the greatest obstacles to the happiness of the Hereafter.

Then He (Exalted) said: ﴿And do not give﴾, O husbands and guardians, ﴿the foolish﴾, that is, from among your wards, your women, and others, ﴿your wealth﴾, that is, the wealth which God created for His servants, whether it is specifically yours or theirs, and you have a connection to it by way of guardianship or otherwise; it is obligatory upon you to preserve it. ﴿Which God has made﴾, that is, He who possesses all-encompassing knowledge and perfect power, ﴿for you a means of support (*qiyam*)﴾, that is, a foundation and pillar by which your affairs stand. Its loss would therefore be a cause of your loss, so its loss is a cause of your ruin. This is naming the cause by the name of its effect, to emphasize its causal role. ﴿And provide for them﴾ from it, while trading with it. He expressed this with the adverbial phrase ﴿from it﴾ to indicate moderation and the investment of wealth, so that it never ceases to be a source of gain, such that the expenditure and clothing come from the profit and not from the capital. ﴿And clothe them﴾, that is, for that is not among what is forbidden, but rather among the noble moral qualities and good deeds. ﴿And speak to them﴾, that is, along with that, ﴿a kind word﴾, that is, one that is acceptable according to the Sharia and reason, such as a good promise and the like, and everything that the soul finds comfort in and loves, whether in word or deed, provided it does not contradict the Sharia; this is "kind." Such speech is often more beneficial than much giving and more effective in cutting off evil. Restraining the foolish person from disposing of his property falls within the scope of this verse, because leaving him unrestrained is among the forbidden "giving."

ولَمّا نَهى عَنْ ذَلِكَ البَذْلِ لِلسُّفَهاءِ؛ أيْتامًا كانُوا؛ أوْ غَيْرَهُمْ؛ بَيَّنَ أنَّهُ لَيْسَ دائِمًا؛ بَلْ ما دامَ السَّفَهُ قائِمًا؛ فَمَسَّتِ الحاجَةُ إلى التَّعْرِيفِ بِمَن يُعْطى؛ ومَن يُمْنَعُ؛ وكَيْفَ يُفْعَلُ عِنْدَ الدَّفْعِ. ولَمّا كانَ السَّفَهُ أمْرًا (p. 197) باطِنًا لا يُعْرَفُ إلّا بِالتَّصَرُّفِ؛ ولا سِيَّما في المالِ؛ بَدَأ - سُبْحانَهُ - بِتَعْلِيمِ ما يَتَوَصَّلُونَ بِهِ إلى مَعْرِفَتِهِ؛ فَقالَ - مُصَرِّحًا بِالأيْتامِ؛ اهْتِمامًا بِأمْرِهِمْ -: ﴿وابْتَلُوا اليَتامى﴾؛ أيْ: اخْتَبِرُوهم في أمْرِ الرُّشْدِ (rushd: الرشد أي حسن التصرف والرشاد) في الدِّينِ؛ والمالِ؛ في مُدَّةِ مُراهَقَتِهِمْ؛ واجْعَلُوا ذَلِكَ دَأْبَكُمْ؛ ﴿حَتّى إذا بَلَغُوا النِّكاحَ﴾؛ أيْ: وقْتَ الحاجَةِ إلَيْهِ؛ بِالِاحْتِلامِ؛ أوِ السِّنِّ؛ ﴿فَإنْ آنَسْتُمْ﴾؛ أيْ: عَلِمْتُمْ عِلْمًا أنْتُمْ في عَظِيمِ تَيَقُّنِهِ؛ كَأنَّكم تُبْصِرُونَهُ عَلى وجْهٍ تُحِبُّونَهُ؛ وتَطِيبُ أنْفُسُكم بِهِ؛ ﴿مِنهُمْ﴾؛ أيْ: عِنْدَ بُلُوغِهِ؛ ﴿رُشْدًا﴾؛ أيْ: بِذَلِكَ التَّصَرُّفِ؛ ونَكَّرَهُ لِأنَّ وُجُودَ كَمالِ الرُّشْدِ في أحَدٍ يَعِزُّ وُقُوعُهُ؛ ﴿فادْفَعُوا إلَيْهِمْ أمْوالَهُمْ﴾؛ أيْ: لِزَوالِ الحاجَةِ إلى الحَجْرِ (hajr: الحجر أي المنع من التصرف في المال) بِخَوْفِ التَّبْذِيرِ؛ وأضافَها إلَيْهِمْ بَعْدَ إضافَتِها أوَّلًا إلى المُعْطِينَ؛ إشارَةً إلى أنَّهُ لا يَسْتَحِقُّها إلّا مَن يُحْسِنُ التَّصَرُّفَ فِيها.

ولَمّا كانَ الإنْسانُ مَجْبُولًا عَلى نَقائِصَ؛ مِنها الطَّمَعُ وعَدَمُ الشِّبَعِ؛ لا سِيَّما إذا خالَطَ؛ لا سِيَّما إنْ حَصَلَ لَهُ إذْنٌ ما؛ أدَّبَهُ - سُبْحانَهُ - بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿ولا تَأْكُلُوها﴾؛ أيْ: بِعِلَّةِ اسْتِحْقاقْكم لِذَلِكَ؛ بِالعَمَلِ فِيها ﴿إسْرافًا﴾؛ أيْ: مُسْرِفِينَ؛ بِالخُرُوجِ عَنِ القَصْدِ في التَّصَرُّفِ؛ ووَضْعِ الشَّيْءِ في غَيْرِ مَوْضِعِهِ؛ وإغْفالِ العَدْلِ؛ والشَّفَقَةِ؛ ﴿وبِدارًا﴾؛ أيْ: مُبادِرِينَ؛ ﴿أنْ يَكْبَرُوا﴾؛ أيْ: فَيَأْخُذُوها مِنكم عِنْدَ كِبَرِهِمْ؛ فَيَفُوتَكم الِانْتِفاعُ بِها؛ وكَأنَّهُ عَطَفَ (p. 198) بِالواوِ الدّالَّةِ عَلى تَمَكُّنِ الوَصْفِ؛ وتَمامِهِ؛ إشارَةً إلى عَدَمِ المُؤاخَذَةِ بِما يَعْجِزُ عَنْهُ الإنْسانُ المَجْبُولُ عَلى النُّقْصانِ؛ مِمّا يُجْرى في الأفْعالِ مُجْرى الوَسْوَسَةِ في الأقْوالِ؛ "ولَنْ يُشادَّ الدِّينَ أحَدٌ إلّا غَلَبَهُ"؛ ولَمّا أشْعَرَ النَّهْيُ عَنْ أكْلِ الكُلِّ؛ بِأنَّ لَهم في الأكْلِ في الجُمْلَةِ عِلَّةً مَقْبُولَةً؛ أفْصَحَ بِهِ في قَوْلِهِ: ﴿ومَن كانَ﴾؛ أيْ: مِنكُمْ؛ أيُّها الأوْلِياءُ؛ ﴿غَنِيًّا فَلْيَسْتَعْفِفْ﴾؛ أيْ: يَطْلُبِ العِفَّةَ؛ ويُوجِدْها؛ ويُظْهِرْها؛ عَنِ الأكْلِ مِنها جُمْلَةً؛ فَيَعِفَّ عَنْهُ بِما بَسَطَ اللَّهُ لَهُ مِن رِزْقِهِ؛ ﴿ومَن كانَ فَقِيرًا﴾؛ وهو يَتَعَهَّدُ مالَ اليَتِيمِ لِإصْلاحِهِ؛ ولَمّا كانَ يُخْشى مِنَ امْتِناعِهِ مِنَ الأكْلِ مِنهُ التَّفْرِيطُ فِيهِ؛ بِالِاشْتِغالِ بِما يُهِمُّهُ في نَفْسِهِ؛ أخْرَجَ الكَلامَ في صِيغَةِ الأمْرِ؛ فَقالَ - مُعَبِّرًا بِالأكْلِ؛ لِأنَّهُ مُعْظَمُ المَقْصُودِ -: ﴿فَلْيَأْكُلْ بِالمَعْرُوفِ﴾؛ أيْ: بِقَدْرِ أُجْرَةِ سَعْيِهِ.

ولَمّا كانَ ذَلِكَ رُبَّما أفْهَمَ الأمانَ إلى الرُّشْدِ؛ بِكُلِّ اعْتِبارٍ؛ أمَرَ بِالحَزْمِ - كَما في الطَّبَرانِيِّ الأوْسَطِ؛ عَنْ أنَسٍ: "احْتَرِسُوا مِنَ النّاسِ بِسُوءِ الظَّنِّ" - فَقالَ: ﴿فَإذا دَفَعْتُمْ إلَيْهِمْ﴾؛ أيْ: اليَتامى؛ ﴿أمْوالَهُمْ﴾؛ أيْ: الَّتِي كانَتْ تَحْتَ أيْدِيكُمْ؛ لِعَجْزِهِمْ عَنْ حِفْظِها؛ ﴿فَأشْهِدُوا عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ (p. 199)؛ أيْ: احْتِياطًا؛ لِأنَّ الأحْوالَ تَتَبَدَّلُ؛ والرُّشْدَ يَتَفاوَتُ؛ فالإشْهادُ أقْطَعُ لِلشَّرِّ؛ وأنْفَعُ في كُلِّ أمْرٍ؛ والأمْرُ بِالإشْهادِ أزْجَرُ لِلْوَلِيِّ عَنِ الخِيانَةِ؛ لِأنَّ مَن عَرَفَ أنَّهُ لا يُقْبَلُ عِنْدَ الخِصامِ إلّا بِبَيِّنَةٍ؛ عَفَّ غايَةَ العِفَّةِ؛ واحْتَرَزَ غايَةَ الِاحْتِرازِ.

ولَمّا كانَتِ الأمْوالُ مَظِنَّةً لِمَيْلِ النُّفُوسِ؛ وكانَ الحُبُّ لِلشَّيْءِ يُعْمِي ويُصِمُّ؛ خَتَمَ الآيَةَ بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿وكَفى بِاللَّهِ﴾؛ أيْ: الَّذِي لَهُ الحِكْمَةُ البالِغَةُ؛ والقُدْرَةُ الباهِرَةُ؛ والعَظَمَةُ الَّتِي لا مِثْلَ لَها؛ والباءُ في مِثْلِ هَذا تَأْكِيدٌ (al-ba' li-l-ta'kid: باء التوكيد)؛ لِأنَّ ما قُرِنَتْ بِهِ هو الفاعِلُ؛ حَقِيقَةً؛ لا مَجازًا؛ كَما إذا أُمِرْنا بِالفِعْلِ؛ مَثَلًا؛ ﴿حَسِيبًا﴾؛ أيْ: مُحاسِبًا؛ بَلِيغًا في الحِسابِ؛ فَهو أبْلَغُ؛ تَحْذِيرًا لَهُمْ؛ ولِلْأيْتامِ؛ مِنَ الخِيانَةِ؛ والتَّعَدِّي؛ ومَدِّ العَيْنِ إلى حَقِّ الغَيْرِ.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 4, verse 7:

When he had mentioned the wealth of orphans, in accordance with what the need called for and what the arrangement (tanasub) required, until he concluded with this verse, it was as if a questioner had asked: "From where will their wealth come?" So he explained that in summary, by His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿For men﴾; that is, the males among the children of the deceased and his relatives. Perhaps He expressed it this way, rather than "the males," because they used not to give inheritance to the young and restricted inheritance to those who defended the dwellings (i.e., the fighters). Thus He (glorified is He) drew attention to the fact that the cause is the bond of lineage, ﴿a share﴾; that is, from them, ﴿is determined﴾; ﴿from what the parents and the relatives leave﴾. And since they used not to give inheritance to women, He said: ﴿And for women is a share﴾. For the sake of explicit statement and emphasis, instead of "from what they left," He said: ﴿from what the parents and the relatives leave﴾, indicating that there is no distinction between them and men in the closeness which is the cause of inheritance. Then he increased the matter in emphasis and explicitness by saying, as a substitution for what precedes it, with the repetition of the governing particle: ﴿from what is little of it or much﴾. Then he made known that this is in the manner of a binding obligation from which there is no escape, so he said, explaining the concern with it by severing it from the first (through the accusative of specification, with the implied "I mean"): ﴿a share ordained﴾; that is, determined, obligatory, specified. This verse is general (mujmal), and the verse of inheritance has explained it; and from the verse it is known that it is specific to the agnatic heirs (asabah), from the expression "ordained" (mafrud), because the consensus, as al-Isbahani transmitted it from al-Razi, is that the kindred by wombs (dhawu al-arham) have no determined share.

When He had explained what is obligatory, He followed it with what is recommended, so He (Exalted is He) said: ﴿And when relatives, orphans and the needy are present at the division, provide for them from it﴾; that is, from among those who do not inherit, whether young or old; ﴿orphans and the needy﴾; that is, whether they are relatives or strangers. ﴿Provide for them from it﴾; that is, from what is left behind. (p-201) This is a command of recommendation (amr nadb), to comfort their hearts; the indication that it turns it away from obligation (wujub) is the absence of any specification. ﴿And speak to them﴾; that is, while giving, ﴿a kind word﴾; that is, good, lawful in the Shariah, accepted, by which their souls are made content.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 4, verse 9:

When He had repeated the injunction concerning orphans once and again, and had concluded with the command to speak gently, and since depiction (taswir) has an effect on the soul that nothing else has, He repeated the injunction concerning them because of their weakness, depicting their condition and making clear that the fair speech (al-qawl al-ma'ruf) is the correct course, in which there is no flaw. So He said: ﴿And let those fear﴾; that is, let them cause fear to arise concerning the offspring of others; ﴿who﴾, and He mentioned for them a state which is worthy of causing fear to arise in their hearts; so He said: ﴿if they were to leave﴾; that is, if they were about to leave (behind), by death or by decrepitude; and He depicted their condition and affirmed it with His saying: ﴿behind them﴾; that is, after their death, or after their incapacity, which is the incapacity that is like their death; ﴿offspring﴾; that is, children, whether male or female; ﴿weak﴾; that is, because of youth or other causes; ﴿they would fear for them﴾; that is, the oppression of oppressors. And since this imagining in their own souls results in their fear for the offspring of others, just as they fear for their own offspring, whether they are guardians (awsiya'), or trustees (awliya'), or strangers (ajanib), and since this fear may lead them, in seeking to benefit them, to oppression of others, He commanded what would keep them upon the straight path, by His saying: ﴿So let them fear God﴾; and He expressed it with the Greatest Name, as guidance toward summoning the whole of His majesty, so He said: ﴿God﴾; that is, let them be just in their affairs, so that God may appoint for them one who will be just to their offspring; otherwise it is likely that He will empower over their offspring one who will oppress them. ﴿And let them speak﴾; that is, concerning that and other matters; ﴿a upright word﴾; that is, justice, aiming at what is right; so that this outward speech may demonstrate the soundness of what is commanded from within.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 4, verse 10:

When the warning, the rebuke, and the terrifying admonition concerning orphans had gone on at length, and this might have caused people to shun contact with them altogether, so that their interests would be lost, He connected to this what makes clear that this (threat) applies specifically to the wrongdoer, in a context that calls for greater warning. So He said, emphasizing what had firmly settled in their souls of making light of their property: ﴿Indeed, those who﴾. And since eating (al-akl) is the greatest aim of a human being, He expressed by it all purposes, saying: ﴿devour the property of orphans unjustly﴾, that is, eating which is out of its proper place, without any proof indicating it, so it is like the act of one who walks in darkness. Then He followed it with what increased its emphasis, by way of warning within a context of restriction (ḥaṣr), saying: ﴿Indeed, they only eat﴾, that is, at present. He depicted the eating and affirmed it by His saying: ﴿into their bellies fire﴾, that is, (p-203) it burns the inner meanings by which the humanness of a human being is sustained. And He made clear that it is in its reality in this world, but we do not perceive it now, because it is not the fire known in its outward sense. By His saying, repeating the warning and clarifying it, with the reading of the majority with the active form (al-bina' lil-fa'il), that they are compelled toward it with a compulsion that makes them as if they were entering it with their own selves: ﴿and they will burn﴾, that is, in the Hereafter, with a certain threat that admits no change; ﴿in a blazing fire﴾, that is, a great one, the utmost in greatness. This is the meaning of the reading of Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim with the passive form (al-bina' lil-majhul), that is, a compelling force compels them to its burning, against which they have no capacity for any kind of defense.

When this was complete, souls longed to know the measures of entitlement to inheritance for each person. The mention of men's and women's entitlement had already preceded, without restriction to orphans. So eloquence required explaining the principles of all inheritance shares, and healing the sick by clarifying the matter. He said, beginning a new sentence (isti'naf) in answer to one who was as if asking about that, emphasizing what He had commanded regarding them to the utmost emphasis, pointing to the greatness of this knowledge by the precedence of the injunction at the beginning of its verses, and the warning against error at its end. The Prophet ﷺ encouraged it by saying that it is half of knowledge, and warned against neglecting it by saying that it is the first knowledge to be taken from the Ummah:

﴿Allah instructs you﴾; that is, with His complete greatness and far-reaching wisdom. He began with the children, because a person's attachment to them is stronger, and so He said: ﴿concerning your children﴾; that is, when their deceased inheritor dies.

Since this was a general statement, it required explanation. So He said, in answer to that, beginning with the most honourable in explanation, to indicate its excellence by placing it first and making it the foundation, and the detail is: ﴿For the male﴾; that is, among them, when there is with him some females, and no impediment prevents him, such as killing or differing in religion or the like: ﴿the equal of the share of two females﴾; that is, a portion which is of a kind that suffices and makes one happy, namely two-thirds when the two females are alone; so for one female with him there is one-third. Thus He, glorified is He, affirmed a share for females, as a severe rebuke to those who prevented them absolutely and reduced them below the share of men, implying that they had gotten the ruling itself right by removing them from the rank of men.

When the share of the male alongside the female was made clear by the explicit wording, and that indicated that females have an inheritance in general, both when alone and when combined with a male, and by the indication of the text (that is what is established by its composition, though it is not intended and the text was not primarily about it), the ruling for two females when there is no male with them was understood, namely that they have two-thirds. This also implied that if one female has a brother with her a third, she has the same with a sister when there is no male there, by way of a fortiori reasoning. Therefore this implied that if they are three or more with no male among them, they exhaust the estate; and if one is alone with no male, she does not get more than a third. He clarified that the matter is not as such, as previously mentioned, by saying, explaining their inheritance when alone: ﴿But if they are﴾; that is, the heirs; ﴿women﴾; that is, females. Since that may be taken to mean the minimum plural, which is two, literally or metaphorically, He established and negated this possibility by saying: ﴿more than two﴾; that is, with no male with them; ﴿for them is two-thirds of what he left﴾; that is, the deceased, and no more than two-thirds. ﴿But if she is﴾; that is, the heiress; ﴿alone﴾; that is, solitary, with no one else with her; ﴿for her is half﴾; that is, only.

Since He had mentioned the injunction concerning children first because of their weakness when they are young, and because the father is the closest of people to the child and the most entitled to its kinship, and the most closely connected to it, He followed it with its ruling, and said: ﴿And for his parents﴾; that is, the deceased. Then He explained after having summarized, so that the speech would be more emphatic and the hearer more eager for it, by saying, substituting for the repetition of the governing word: ﴿for each one of them﴾; that is, his father and his mother, who are referred to in the dual as "two parents" (p-206): ﴿a sixth of what he left﴾. Then He explained the condition for that, and said: ﴿if he has﴾; that is, the deceased; ﴿children﴾; that is, a male. If it is a female, the father takes a sixth as a fixed share, and the remainder after the fixed shares goes to him as a residuary right (ʿuṣūba).

When He had explained their ruling with children, He followed it with the case of their absence, and said: ﴿But if he has no children﴾; that is, male or female; ﴿and his parents inherit from him﴾; that is, only them; ﴿then for his mother is one-third﴾; that is, and for the father the remainder, because the premise is that he has no heir other than them both. Since the implied sense was "this also applies with the absence of siblings," He built on it His saying: ﴿But if he has siblings﴾; that is, two or more, male or not, with the absence of children; ﴿then for his mother is a sixth﴾; that is, because the siblings reduce her from a third to it, and the remainder goes to the father, and they get nothing. As for a single sister, she does not reduce her to a sixth, whether she is an heir or not; similarly a single brother. Then He explained that all of this is after the execution of the bequest and the debt, because the right of the deceased who gathered the wealth takes precedence in that, and so He said: ﴿after a bequest he makes or a debt﴾; that is, as is recommended for every dead person. He placed it first in wording, though it takes precedence over it in the law, to encourage its fulfilment, because the hearts of the heirs are stingy with it, since it is like their sharing in the inheritance, for it is without compensation. ﴿Or a debt﴾; that is, if there is (p-207) a debt upon him.

Since a person may see that some of his relatives, whether ascendants, descendants or others, are more beneficial to him, and so he loves to prefer them, he transgresses these limits on account of what he sees. But what he sees is contrary to the truth in the present or in the outcome. Allah (exalted is He) is the one who alone holds the knowledge of that. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "Love your beloved moderately, for he may one day become your enemy, and hate your enemy moderately, for he may one day become your beloved," and the hadith continues, because hearts are between two fingers of the fingers of the Merciful, He turns them however He wills. He (exalted is He) said, urging adherence to what He has set as limits, emphasizing with the parenthetical clause (al-jumla al-i'tirāḍiyya) — as is the case with every parenthesis — because this division differs from what the Arabs used to do, and it has aspects whose causes cannot be grasped: ﴿Your fathers and your sons﴾; that is, those whose inheritance We have explained to you as We have mentioned; ﴿you do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit﴾; that is, more than the other, for you have no comprehensive knowledge nor power. So if the matter of division were left to you, you would not have placed matters in their most fitting places.

When He had explained that the inheritance is as He, glorified and exalted is He, has set it, emphasizing it with the word "bequest," and reinforcing it further by what He made a parenthesis between the injunction and the word "obligation," He made clear that it is by way of binding decree, whoever abandons it disobeys. So He said, mentioning a verbal noun (maṣdar) derived from the meaning of the speech (p-208): ﴿an obligation from Allah﴾; that is, the One to whom all command belongs. Then He increased them in urging and desire regarding it, by saying, giving the reason for His obligation upon them absolutely and in this manner: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾; that is, the One encompassing in knowledge and power; ﴿is﴾; and has always been and always will be, because His existence does not vary at any time, since time does not pass over Him, nor does place contain Him, for He is the creator of both; ﴿Knowing﴾; that is, of the consequences; ﴿Wise﴾; that is, He laid down these rulings for you to the utmost perfection, in bringing benefits to you and repelling harm from you. He arranged them, glorified and exalted is He, in the best order, for the heir is connected to the deceased sometimes through an intermediary, which is the kalāla, and sometimes without an intermediary; and this latter is sometimes by lineage, and sometimes by marriage and lineage. So He put first what is without an intermediary, for its great closeness, began with lineage among them for its strength, and began among them with the child, for greater care for it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 4, verse 12:

Since inheritance through marriage (*al-irth bil-musaharah*) is weaker than inheritance through blood kinship (*al-irth bil-qarabah*), he mentions it after the latter. He places it before inheritance through fraternal kinship, to draw attention to its importance, and because it is without an intermediary. He mentions the husband first, because he is the more excellent. So He says: ﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave﴾. He specifies the condition of this by His saying: ﴿if they have no child﴾, meaning, of yours or of others. Then He states the ruling for the other case, saying: ﴿But if they have a child﴾, meaning an heir, however remote, whether a son or a daughter, ﴿then for you is a fourth of what they leave﴾, meaning what each of them leaves. The husband washes her (*yughassiluha*), because God attributed her to him by the name of marriage (*al-zawjiyyah*), and the original meaning is the literal one. The prohibition on intercourse with her after death does not harm this, nor does the permissibility of marrying her sister or four others (after her death), because that is due to the absence of the cause (*muqtada*) or the presence of an impediment (*mani'*), which is life. That does not prevent the bond of marriage that permits the washing, just as it did not prevent it for the sake of the waiting period (*'iddah*) had the separation been by divorce. Then He repeats the ruling on the bequest, out of concern for its matter, saying: ﴿after any bequest they make or debt﴾, meaning the wives, or some of them. Perhaps He gathered it (in the plural) to indicate that the bequest is a great matter, which should be kept in mind and not overlooked by anyone among people.

When he had explained the man's inheritance, he followed it with the woman's inheritance, saying, informing that it is half of what is due to the husband, as was stated for children: ﴿And for them﴾, meaning whether they are many or one, ﴿is a fourth of what you leave﴾, meaning they share it equally if they are many, and one of them has it alone if there is no other. Then He specified its condition by His saying: ﴿if you have no child﴾. Then He stated the ruling for the other case by His saying: ﴿But if you have a child﴾, meaning an heir, ﴿then for them is an eighth of what you leave﴾, as was mentioned for the fourth. Then He repeated the exception to the rights of the deceased, saying: ﴿after any bequest you make or debt﴾.

When He had finished the two divisions concerning what is directly connected to the deceased, He followed it with the third, which is what is connected through an intermediary. Since it has two divisions, for it sometimes connects through the mother alone, and these are the *akhyaf* (uterine siblings), whose mother is one but whose fathers differ; and sometimes through the father alone, and these are the *'illat* (consanguine siblings), whose father is one but whose mothers differ; and sometimes through both parents, and these are the *a'yan* (full siblings). Since fraternal kinship is weaker than the kinship of descent (*al-bunuwwah*), He reinforced it by what its state requires, and so He placed it in two accounts. He mentioned one of them here, to include it within the ruling of the prescribed bequest, and He concluded the surah with the other, because conclusions are among the places of concern.

Since maternal kinship is weaker than paternal kinship, He placed it first here, as an indication of concern for its matter, and that what they used to do of depriving females is an error and a deviation from the path of justice. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if there is a man who is inherited by *kalalah*﴾, meaning, if there is found a man who is inherited in the state of *kalalah*, meaning one who has no child in that state, nor a parent. Or *yurathu* may be from *uriltha* (passive voice), meaning that the inheritance of the heir is through the one who died in such a state, who is neither a child nor a parent of the deceased. And his heir is also a *kalalah*, since he is neither a parent nor a child. So the deceased is the *kalalah* of his heir, and the heir is the *kalalah* of his deceased. Al-Asfahani said: "A man (who is) *kalalah*," "a woman (who is) *kalalah*," and "people (who are) *kalalah*" are not made dual or plural, because it is a verbal noun (*masdar*), like *al-dalalah* and *al-wakalah*, and it has the meaning of *al-kalal*, which is the loss of strength from exhaustion. The term *kalalah* is sometimes applied to kinship from a direction other than child or parent, and from this is the saying of the people: "He did not inherit glory from *kalalah*" (i.e., not from direct ancestry). ﴿Or﴾ there is found ﴿a woman﴾, meaning who is inherited in the same way. It is possible that *yurathu* is a descriptive attribute (*sifah*) and *kalalatan* is the predicate of *kana*. ﴿And he has﴾, meaning the aforementioned, who is the one inherited, in whichever of the two states he is. Since the basis of being a relative through pure femininity is equal between male and female, because of its weakness, He said: ﴿a brother or a sister﴾, meaning from the mother, by the consensus of the exegetes, and this is the reading of Ubayy and Sa'd ibn Malik, may God be pleased with them both. ﴿Then for each one of them is a sixth﴾, meaning of his estate, without preference for the male over the female.

When that is understood, namely by altering the wording so that it is not said "then for him is a sixth" (that they, if they are together, have a third), and this might be understood to mean that if the heirs increase, the inheritance increases beyond a third, He negated that by His saying: ﴿But if they are more than that﴾, meaning more than one, however they may be, among the heirs of that kind (as understood from "a brother or a sister"), ﴿then they are partners﴾, meaning equally, ﴿in the third﴾, meaning the total made up of the two sixths, which were previously mentioned as being between them. They are not given anything more than that. Then He repeated the urging to safeguard the interest of the deceased, as a clarification of concern for it, saying: ﴿after any bequest that is made or debt﴾.

Since the deceased may harm his heirs, or some of them, by something that removes it from them, openly or secretly, such as acknowledging his wealth to a stranger, or acknowledging a debt that has no reality, or a debt he had but claiming that he had settled it, He concluded the verse with a warning against that, by His saying: ﴿without causing harm﴾, along with what was previously indicated at the beginning of the account by His saying: ﴿You do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit﴾ [al-Nisa': 11]. Al-Asfahani said: "Harm in a bequest is among the major sins." Then He reinforced that by saying, as a verbal noun (*masdar*), in order that He might enjoin upon you: ﴿a bequest from God﴾, meaning He who has all authority, together with His emphasis on it through all that is in the verses, magnifying the matter by encompassing the bequest at its beginning and its end. It is less than the obligatory share with respect to children, because their right is more emphatic.

When He, glorified is He, had explained the principles and resolved the dispute, and this was contrary to what they were accustomed to, and weaning from what one is accustomed to is at the peak of hardship, the situation required admonition through encouragement and warning. So He concluded the account by His saying: ﴿And God﴾, meaning the One who combines the attributes of perfection, of majesty and of beauty. And to indicate the greatness of the bequest, He repeated this greatest name throughout the account. Then He said: ﴿is Knowing﴾, meaning nothing of the affair of whoever disobeys is hidden from Him, whether by word or deed, intention or otherwise. ﴿Forbearing﴾: it is of His nature not to hasten punishment, so one should not be deceived by His granting respite, for when He seizes after long patience, He does not let go. So beware of the anger of the Forbearing. In the combination of the two attributes with the warning, there is an attraction toward repentance.

When the weaning of their souls from withholding from children and women was difficult for them, because they had become accustomed to it through the passing of long ages, persisting in its practice and deeming it good, He—glorified be He—followed it with encouragement and warning, lest anyone be deceived by the attribute of Forbearing (al-Halim). He said, glorifying the matter with the particle of distance and indicating all that preceded of the matters of inheritance, women, orphans, and other things:

﴿That﴾: i.e., these sublime limits, great in benefit and far-reaching in outcome, mentioned from the beginning of this surah, indeed from the beginning of the Qur'an. ﴿are the limits of Allah﴾: i.e., of the Greatest King. So whoever observes them—even if he does not intend obedience to Him, but rather to elevate himself above the baseness of clinging to the perishable and the disgrace of monopolizing from the weak, which indicates stinginess and lowness of aspiration—attains a great good, for it is likely that this will draw him to become one of those who obey Allah. ﴿And whoever obeys Allah﴾: the One possessing the two attributes of Majesty and Honor; ﴿and His Messenger﴾: i.e., in all his acts of obedience, these and others, by turning towards them and abandoning whatever is other than them for His sake—glorified be He. Al-Isfahani said: "Man" (من) is general, and its occurrence after these specific obligations does not restrict it.

When the listener's whole attention had become eager for the announcement, He turned to it, magnifying the matter—according to the reading of Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir with the nun—saying: ﴿He will admit him to gardens﴾: i.e., orchards. The reading of the majority with the ya' is also magnificent, for its construction upon the Greatest Name, although this one is more stimulating with the pleasure of the shift (of pronoun). ﴿Beneath which rivers flow﴾: i.e., because its land is a source of waters; wherever you wish, a river flows, so it remains ever fresh and luxuriant. He gathered those who attain entry into Paradise in His saying: ﴿abiding therein﴾, giving glad tidings of the abundance of those who stand by these limits; and because companionship with brothers is among the highest bliss of the Gardens.

When their being singled out for inheritance over women and children was among their successes, indeed the great success for them was nothing but possessing wealth and attaining what was in mind of hopes from it, He—exalted be He—said, magnifying with the particle of distance: ﴿And that﴾: i.e., the matter of lofty rank, of obedience recommended; ﴿is the great success﴾: i.e., not other than it, from possessing what Allah has not permitted. This is the most fitting thing for placing encouragement first, so that their souls may be willing to abandon what they were engaged in, along with what it contains of gentleness toward this community and the good news to him ﷺ that it is obedient and rightly guided.

Now that the pure hearts, possessed of lofty aspirations, had been given a taste of their love for attaining this triumph, he followed it with a warning, weaning them completely away from those benefits. So He said: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah﴾, i.e., He to whom all greatness belongs; ﴿and His Messenger﴾, i.e., in that and other matters; ﴿and transgresses His limits﴾, i.e., the limits He set in these rulings and others. He put the disobedient one in the singular when speaking of the Fire, in His saying: ﴿He will admit him to a Fire, to abide therein forever﴾, because isolation, which entails desolation, is part of the punishment and humiliation. And since their withholding of inheritance from women and children was a matter of contempt for them, He concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿And for him is a humiliating punishment﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 4, verse 15:

When He, glorified be He, had preceded (this) in the enjoining of (good treatment of) women, and goodness in this world is sometimes by reward and sometimes by reprimand and reproach, because the basis of the sacred laws (shara'i') is justice and equity and avoiding, in every matter, the two extremes of excess (ifrat) and neglect (tafrit) — and He, glorified be He, concluded with the humiliation of the disobedient, as a kindness to him, by restraining him from corruption, lest that cast him into destruction forever and ever — and among the most heinous acts of disobedience was fornication (zina), and corruption among women was greater, the temptation through them greater, and the harm from them more dangerous, and they may introduce to men someone who inherits from them who is not of their offspring — He gave precedence to them in this, out of concern for restraining them. So He said: ﴿And those who⦆; it is the plural of "allati" (the feminine relative pronoun). Perhaps He expressed them in the plural as an indication of their multitude, just as He indicated that in ﴿two, three, or four﴾ [an-Nisa': 3], and (as an indication) of the abundance of corruption from them. ﴿Commit⦆; that is, they do — by mentioning the cause for the effect, and expressing it this way is more eloquent — ﴿the immorality⦆; that is, the act of extreme abomination. And in the verse — because among the greatest intended meanings of its arrangement, following the verses of inheritance and what preceded them, is the safeguarding of lineage — there is an indication, by mentioning the punishment of the adulteress without addressing the inheritance of the child born from her, that the child belongs to the marriage bed, and that it is not denied on mere suspicion, but only after certainty, as in Surat an-Nur, because the existence of adultery does not necessarily entail the denial of the child, and its being from adultery. Abu Hayyan said in "al-Nahr": "Here 'al-fahisha' is adultery, by the consensus of the exegetes, except what Mujahid held, and whom Abu Muslim al-Isfahani followed, that it is lesbianism (musahaqa), and among men, sodomy (liwat)." Then he clarified the relative clause by his saying: ﴿from your women⦆; that is, free women; ﴿then call to witness against them⦆; that is, seek that you have them testify; ﴿four⦆; from among the men.

Since He, exalted be He, had made this Community a middle nation, who turn to others while others do not turn to them, He said: ﴿from among you⦆; that is, from among the upright Muslims, (testifying) that they committed it; ﴿and if they testify⦆; that is, to that; ﴿then confine them⦆; that is, detain them; ﴿in the houses⦆; that is, and prevent them from going out, for that is more protective of them; and let this restriction continue; ﴿until death takes them⦆; that is, comes upon them while they are still preserved in their honor; ﴿or God⦆, whose knowledge and wisdom encompass all, ﴿makes for them a way⦆; that is, a way out before death, through the clarification of the prescribed punishment (hadd), or through marriage.
