That is, a firm covenant that you will not fight them and will not fight whoever takes refuge with them, or enters into what they have entered into; so refrain at that time from seizing them and killing them. ﴿Or﴾ those who ﴿come to you﴾ in a state in which their ﴿hearts are restrained﴾, that is, constricted, timid and reluctant, ﴿from﴾, that is, from ﴿fighting you﴾, that is, for the sake of their religion and their people, ﴿or fighting their own people﴾, that is, for your sake, fleeing from fighting you and fighting their people; so do not seize them and do not fight them, because they are like those at peace by abstaining from fighting. Perhaps he used the past tense in ﴿came﴾ (jā'a) as an indication (p-358) that the condition for their equality with those who join the people of the covenant is that this not be repeated; if it is repeated by them, then they are the others whose ruling will come.

Since the implied sense is: "If Allah had willed, He would have made them one bloc with their people against you," He followed it with His saying: ﴿And if﴾, that is, the meaning is: while the situation is that ﴿if Allah had willed﴾, that is, He who is characterized by every perfection, ﴿He would have empowered them﴾, that is, these joiners and comers in that state from among the disbelievers, ﴿over you﴾, varying among the kinds of empowerment; an empowerment proceeding according to causes and the established course, because they have strength to fight you, ﴿so they would have fought you﴾, that is, this empowerment would have resulted in their fighting you, alone or together with others of your enemies. The lam in it is the answer to "if" (law), by repetition, or as a substitution for "empowered" (sallaṭa).

Since what was conditioned upon was the prohibition of fighting them at that time, he stated it explicitly in His saying: ﴿So if they withdraw from you﴾, that is, these whom I commanded you to refrain from, from among the hypocrites, ﴿and do not fight you﴾, alone or joined with others, ﴿and offer you peace﴾, that is, submission; ﴿then Allah has not given you any way against them﴾, that is, the One (p-359) for whom no one has any command in any direction, to seize them or kill them.

Al-Biqa'i, *Nazm al-Durar*, commentary on Surah 4, verse 91:

As though it were said: "Is there any remaining category of the hypocrites?" It is said: "Yes." ﴿You will find others﴾; that is, soon, by a promise that is beyond doubt. ﴿Others﴾; that is, from among the hypocrites. ﴿Who wish to be safe from you﴾; that is, so that no harm comes to you from them. ﴿And to be safe from their own people﴾; likewise, because of their weakness before each of you. So they show you faith when they meet you, and they show disbelief when they meet their own people. This is the meaning of ﴿Whenever they are returned to temptation﴾; that is, to being tested by fear when they mix with others. ﴿They are plunged back into it﴾; that is, they are turned upside down, head over heels, ﴿into it﴾.

Since these people were more deeply rooted in hypocrisy, more corrupt, lower, and more hostile than those before them, He stated the implication of what He had stated about those (earlier) people, because their case is more severe, and they are more deserving of severity than the first group. He omitted what He had stated explicitly. Then He said: ﴿So if they do not withdraw from you﴾. Since withdrawal (i'tizal) is an act of submission and not of arrogance, He stated it explicitly in His words: ﴿and offer you peace﴾; that is, submission. Since the offering of peace must have indicators by which it is recognised, He said: ﴿and restrain their hands﴾; that is, from fighting you and harming you. ﴿Then seize them﴾; that is, overpower them with every kind of overpowering that you are able to exercise. ﴿And kill them﴾ (p. 360). Since their hypocrisy, as previously mentioned, is at the utmost degree of vileness, and their characters are at the extreme of baseness, He pointed to the promise of making it easy for you to gain control over them, and so He said: ﴿wherever you find them﴾. Its meaning is: you encounter them and overtake them while you are victorious over them, skilful in fighting them, alert to it, and agile in it, for the word *thaqif* means the skilful, the agile, and the alert. For this reason He referred to them with the particle of distance, saying: ﴿those﴾; that is, those far removed from attaining mercy, from victory, from salvation, and from every good. ﴿We have given﴾; that is, by Our greatness. ﴿To you against them clear authority﴾; that is, domination; ﴿clear﴾; that is, manifest in its strength and its dominance.

These verses are abrogated (mansukhah) by the verse of "Bara'ah" (Surah 9), because it was revealed later, after Tabuk.

When he had explained their categories, with an explanation that made clear their conditions are confusing, and had commanded fighting them while striving to ascertain their conditions, and had concluded with empowering (the believers) over them, and since it might happen that someone who does not deserve to be killed would be killed because of the confusion, he followed this with his saying, the purpose of which is prohibition, presenting it in the form of an emphatic negation with the word "kāna" (it is not) in order to intensify the deterrence against it, because of the motives that drive souls to killing when their desires are aroused: ﴿It is not for a believer﴾; that is, it is forbidden for him; ﴿to kill a believer﴾; that is, in any circumstance whatsoever; ﴿except by mistake﴾; that is, in the case of error, by not intending to kill, or not intending that particular person, or intending him with something not intended to take life, or not intending what is prohibited, such as one who shoots at the ranks of the unbelievers while a Muslim is among them, or by being one who is not legally responsible. Killing in this manner is not forbidden. What he mentioned here, in the categories of the hypocrites, is an indication that one should be careful and diligent in every matter of killing whenever it is possible that the killer is a believer, a possibility that custom does not render close. From this it follows that the ruling on mistaken killing must be explained. The lam of exclusivity (in "li") may be used for what is not prohibited, as in: "For it is only yours, or your brother's, or the wolf's." It seems that he expressed it thus in order to convey, through the obligation of expiation and blood-money, the utmost deterrence from killing a believer, for if this is the recompense for what is (legally) one's own, what is to be thought of what is not one's own? Then He (Exalted is He) said: ﴿And whoever kills a believer﴾, whether young or old, male or female. Perhaps He, glorified and exalted, expressed it by this attribute as an admonition that if he is not such in reality, then nothing is due from him in reality, even if he is bound by it outwardly; ﴿by mistake﴾. Since error has been lifted from this community, one might suppose that nothing is owed by the one who errs. He therefore clarified that the matter of killing is not like that, in order to preserve souls, because the matter concerning them is extremely grave. So He said, intensifying (the ruling) against him and urging greater reflection and care when doing what may cause death: ﴿then (the freeing of) a neck﴾; that is, it is obligatory upon him to free ﴿a neck﴾; that is, a soul, which He expressed by "neck" because a soul cannot live without it (the neck); ﴿believing﴾; even if by selling a house or orchards; ﴿free of what would impair work﴾. He placed the freeing here first, as an encouragement to mend what has been breached of the servant's (protective) veil. To make this obligatory in the case of error is, a fortiori, to make it obligatory in the case of intention. It seems that he did not mention it in the case of intentional killing because that is lighter in general, while the context is one of intensification. ﴿And a blood-money paid﴾; that is, paid with ease and facility; ﴿to his family﴾; that is, his heirs, who divide it as inheritance is divided; ﴿unless they waive it﴾; that is, it is obligatory upon him in every case, except when they give it as charity by pardoning the killer, by releasing him from the blood-money, in which case nothing is due from him then. He expressed it as "charity" to encourage it. ﴿But if he was﴾; that is, the one killed; ﴿from a people﴾; that is, among them is strength; ﴿hostile to you﴾; that is, fighting against you; ﴿and he was﴾; that is, while the situation is that he was ﴿a believer, then (the freeing of) a believing neck﴾; that is, it is obligatory upon the killer to free ﴿a believing neck﴾. It seems that He expressed it thus as an indication of care regarding the soundness of her (the freed slave's) Islam. This (situation) has removed the sanctity of his own life without expiation, by his dwelling in the abode of war, which is the abode of permissibility, or by his being in their ranks, or by his being counted among them. He said "from" (min). Its meaning, as al-Shafi'i and others said, following Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is: in "and if he was", that is, the one killed; "from a people", that is, unbelievers too; "hostile to you"; "between you and them there is a covenant", and he is an unbeliever like them; "then a blood-money", that is, what is obligatory for him is, as with the believer mentioned before, ("a blood-money paid to his family"), according to his religion: if he is a People of the Book, then a third of the blood-money of a Muslim; if he is a Magian, then two-thirds of a tenth of it; "and (the freeing of) a believing neck." It seems that He placed the blood-money first here as an indication of hastening to pay it, to preserve the covenant, and to confirm the matter of freeing by making it a conclusion, just as it was an opening, as an encouragement to fulfil it, because it is a trust, for which no claimant exists except Allah. Al-Asfahani said: the secret of this is that its obligation in the case of a believer is more fitting than the blood-money, and the reverse here; end of quotation.

The secret of this lies in looking to the good of religion regarding the believer, and to the preservation of the covenant regarding the unbeliever. ﴿So whoever does not find (a neck)﴾; that is, the slave, nor anything by which to attain it; ﴿then fasting﴾; that is, it is obligatory upon him to fast ﴿two consecutive months﴾; so that if he breaks it for a single day without menstruation or postpartum bleeding, he must begin again. He gave the reason for this by his saying, counting the error (as a sin) after expressing it with the lam which implies that it is permissible, as a sin, in order to intensify the urging toward greater caution: ﴿a repentance﴾; that is, He prescribed this for you for the sake of accepting repentance; ﴿from Allah﴾; that is, the Supreme King, in whose grip is everything.

Since expiations involve great hardship upon the soul, He encouraged them, glorified and exalted is He, by concluding the verse with His saying: ﴿And Allah is﴾; that is, the One encompassing all attributes of perfection; (p. 364) ﴿Knowing﴾; that is, of what sets you right in this world and the next, and of what occurs as error in reality or intentionally; so no one should be deceived by the establishment of rulings according to outward appearance; ﴿Wise﴾; in His establishing deterrents through expiations and other means. So adhere to His commands and keep far from His prohibitions, that you may attain knowledge and wisdom.

When (Exalted is He) addressed the error as He would address what belongs to the doer, thereby making people averse to it with this strong aversion, it was most appropriate for Him to mention what is not part of that (error). For controlling the self after it has been let loose is very difficult. Often, a grudge makes it easy to kill someone whose Islam has been established, and resentment drives a person toward him, and the strength of one's temperament strengthens doubts about him. By my life, restraining oneself from action after having been let loose is harder than urging oneself toward boldness. Only one who has tested souls at the moment of nearing victory, and at the pleasure of revenge while having power and capability, knows this.

So He said: ﴿And whoever kills a believer﴾. Perhaps by using the present tense (muḍāriʿ, the imperfect verb form) He indicated the continuation of the determination to do that for the sake of the faith, and that this cannot be anything but disbelief. He left the speech open to admit additional aversion from killing a Muslim: ﴿intentionally﴾, meaning that as for the error, its ruling has already been mentioned concerning the believer and others. ﴿Then his recompense﴾, meaning for that, ﴿is Hell﴾, meaning it will receive him in a very hideous state, just as the one killed was made to frown (tajahhama, to show a grim face). ﴿Abiding therein﴾, meaning remaining for an endless duration. ﴿And Allah became angry﴾, meaning the Supreme King to whom none is equal, in addition to that, ﴿with him and has cursed him﴾, meaning and has removed him far from His mercy. ﴿And has prepared for him a great punishment﴾, meaning whose reality your minds cannot reach.

If the statement in this verse is taken in its general sense, then what specifies it is what precedes and follows it, from His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa’: 48]. It is not the verse of "al-Furqan," for that is Meccan (makki), and this one is Medinan (madani).

When this strict prohibition against deliberately killing a believer had been made clear, along with the sin in unintentional killing that calls for caution, and since the command concerned fighting and killing in jihad, which was emphasized in various ways, the situation could sometimes become confused. So he followed this with an explicit command to exercise care, as an answer to one who seems to have asked: "What should we do between the two matters of advancing and holding back?" He said: ﴿O you who believe﴾. By using the particle of distance and the past tense, which is the lowest of the forms of address, he indicated that the firmly grounded do not need further emphasis in being disciplined. How well he turned to His saying: ﴿And urge the believers﴾ [al-Nisa': 84], indicating that they are moved by his exhortation (ﷺ) and submit to his command, as shown by the word "when" in His saying: ﴿When you travel﴾, meaning: when you journey and go about in the land, ﴿in the way of Allah﴾, meaning: the One to whom belongs all perfection, for His sake alone, sincerely, ﴿then investigate﴾, meaning: seek, with deliberation and care, the clarification of matters, the steadiness in dealing with them, and great caution when taking them up, which means distinguishing one thing from another and removing their ambiguity completely. Do not proceed except in what has become clear to you. ﴿And do not say﴾, meaning: any word, let alone what is higher than that, ﴿to one who offers you peace﴾, meaning: whoever he is, ﴿peace﴾, meaning: he hastened to greet you with the greeting of Islam, surrendering his submission, ﴿you are not a believer﴾, meaning: rather he seeks refuge, so that you may kill him.

Since pursuing desires was among the Arabs an extremely blameworthy thing, he said, rebuking and warning against the like of this, in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the subject of "say": ﴿seeking﴾, meaning: while you are eagerly striving ﴿to kill him﴾, meaning: to take what he has of the perishable goods and the passing possessions, or to obtain vengeance that you had against him. Al-Bukhari, in his Tafsir, and Muslim, at the end of his book, related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "﴿And do not say to one who offers you peace﴾. He said: A man was with his flock, and the Muslims caught up with him, and he said: 'Peace be upon you.' So they killed him and took his flock. Then Allah, glorified and exalted is He, revealed concerning that, up to His saying: ﴿the goods of this worldly life﴾." Al-Harith ibn Abi Usama related it from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, adding: ﴿Thus you were before﴾, concealing your faith while you were among the polytheists, ﴿then Allah bestowed favor upon you﴾, and made Islam manifest, ﴿so investigate﴾.

Then he gave the reason for the prohibition of this condition by His saying: ﴿With Allah are abundant spoils﴾, meaning: the One to whom belongs majesty and honor will make you independent by them of what you seek of worldly goods, along with their goodness. Then he gave the reason for the prohibition at its root by His saying: ﴿Thus﴾, meaning: like this man whom you killed, by your considering him far from Islam, ﴿you were﴾, and he limited the time of the killing, as is the reality, by His saying: ﴿before﴾, meaning: before you uttered the word of Islam, ﴿then Allah bestowed favor﴾, meaning: the One who possesses all the attributes of perfection, ﴿upon you﴾, meaning: by casting into the hearts of the believers the acceptance of what you displayed, in compliance with His command, glorified and exalted is He, to that effect. Thus He strengthened the matter of faith in your hearts little by little, until you reached the state you are in, in firmness in the religion, fame through it, and honor. Had He willed, He would have hardened your hearts and empowered them over you, so they would have killed you. When the matter is thus, you must treat those who enter the religion with the acceptance that He showed to you. This is the meaning of what he made the consequence of the admonition, by His saying, emphasizing what has passed and announcing the gravity of the matter of killing: ﴿so investigate﴾, meaning: the matters, and be steadfast in them until they become clear. Then he gave a reason for this command by His saying, encouraging and warning: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾, meaning: the One singled out as the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, ﴿Acquainted﴾, meaning: He knows what you have undertaken, whether with clarity or otherwise. So beware of Him by guarding your inner selves and your outward conduct.

When this verse was linked to what preceded it, the verse about deliberate killing, and it turned toward ﴿Urge the believers﴾ [An-Nisa 4:84] and toward the verse of greeting, its attachment to them grew strong. It became known from them that striving in the way of God (jihad) carries this danger, so one might sometimes grow lax in it. It clarified its merit for one who was, as it were, saying: "Then at that point we will sit out the jihad so that we may be safe," by His saying: ﴿Those who sit [at home] are not equal﴾, meaning, from jihad, ﴿among the believers﴾, meaning those fully immersed in faith. This serves to state explicitly the preference of the believing fighter (mujahid) over the believing one who sits, lest anyone single him out as an unbelieving denier.

Since there were among people those whom He, glory be to Him, excused by His mercy, He made an exception for them. (p-369) So He said, describing those who sit or excepting them from it: ﴿other than those with a harm﴾, meaning one who is prevented or hindered from jihad in the way of God, by a limp, illness, blindness, or the like. By this it becomes clear that the discourse concerns the emigrants (muhajirun). In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, in the Book of Tafsir (exegesis), it is related from Zayd ibn Thabit, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ dictated to him: "Those who sit [at home] among the believers are not equal to those who strive in the way of Allah," and Ibn Umm Maktum came to him while he was dictating it to me. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, by Allah, if I could fight, I would fight," and he was blind. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent down to His Messenger, while his thigh was upon my thigh, and it became heavy on me until I feared my thigh would be crushed. Then the tranquility (sakina) lifted from him, and Allah revealed: ﴿other than those with a harm﴾.

Al-Bukhari also related it in the Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an from al-Bara', may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "When ﴿Those who sit [at home] are not equal﴾, the verse, was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Call Zayd for me, and let him bring the tablet, the inkwell, and the shoulder-blade,' then he said: 'Write.'" Then he mentioned it.

The hadith of Zayd was also related by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Nasa'i. In the narration of Abu Dawud, he said: "I was beside the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when tranquility overcame him, and the thigh of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ fell upon my thigh. I found nothing heavier than the thigh of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Then the tranquility lifted from him, and he said to me: 'Write.'" (p-370) So I wrote on a shoulder-blade: ﴿Those who sit [at home] are not equal﴾ to the end of it. Then Ibn Umm Maktum, who was a blind man, stood up when he heard the excellence of the fighters, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, what of one among the believers who cannot fight?" When he had finished his speech, the tranquility overcame the Messenger of Allah ﷺ again, and his thigh fell upon my thigh. I found its weight the second time just as I had found it the first time. Then the tranquility lifted from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and he said: "Read, O Zayd." So I read: ﴿Those who sit [at home] among the believers are not equal﴾, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: ﴿other than those with a harm﴾, the whole verse. Zayd said: "Allah revealed it alone, so I added it. By Him in whose hand is my soul, it is as if I can see its addition at the crack in the shoulder-blade." Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shayba and Abu Ya'la al-Mawsili also related it, and in it: "When revelation came down upon the Prophet ﷺ, his gaze would become fixed, his eyes open, and he would empty his hearing and heart for what came to him from Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

When He mentioned the one who sits, He followed it with its counterpart, the fighter, by His saying: ﴿And those who strive in the way of Allah﴾, meaning the religion of the Supreme King, whoever follows it reaches His mercy, ﴿with their wealth and their selves﴾. Since negating equality could lead each of the two groups to expect preference, because the one who sits, though he has missed jihad, has nonetheless stayed behind the fighter with his family, since he gives life to the religion by occupying himself with knowledge and the like, He said, resuming: (p-371) ﴿God has preferred﴾, meaning He who possesses the attributes of perfection, ﴿the fighters﴾. Since wealth was scarce at the beginning of the matter, He placed wealth first, saying: ﴿with their wealth and their selves﴾, meaning jihad actually carried out, ﴿over those who sit [at home]﴾, meaning those who refrain from that while being able to do it, by their being in the abode of emigration, ﴿a degree﴾, meaning one degree, complete, because they did not surpass them by anything else.

In al-Bukhari, in the Book of the Campaigns (al-Maghazi), it is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them: "Those who sit [at home] among the believers, other than the people of Badr, and those who went out to Badr, are not equal."

When He joined the fighters and those who sit together by His saying: ﴿And to each﴾, meaning of the two categories, ﴿God has promised﴾, meaning He who is encompassed by majesty and honor, a reward for their faith, ﴿the best﴾, He clarified that the sitter who participates is only the one who has the near power of jihad, which is the ability to carry out the command, by reason of his emigration to the land of war and his being among the people of faith. As for one who sits out from emigration while able to do it, he is not a participant in that, rather he is a wrongdoer to himself, for he is not able to carry out the commands, so he is neither a fighter in actuality nor in near potential. So He said: ﴿And God has preferred﴾, meaning the King to whom none is equal, so He cannot be compelled, ﴿the fighters﴾, meaning in actuality absolutely, with self or with wealth, ﴿over those who sit [at home]﴾, meaning those who refrain from the means enabling jihad and emigration, ﴿a great reward﴾.

Then He clarified it by His saying: ﴿degrees﴾; and He magnified them by His saying: ﴿from Him﴾. These degrees are the degree of emigration (hijrah); the degree of being able to engage in jihad after the emigration; and the degree of actually engaging in jihad in deed.

Since a person is never free from slips, however diligent he is in his deeds, He said: ﴿and forgiveness﴾; that is, the erasing of their sins, such that they are not mentioned and are not requited for; ﴿and mercy﴾; that is, honor and elevation; ﴿and Allah is ever﴾; that is, the One encompassing the Most Beautiful Names and the Lofty Attributes; ﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾; eternally and everlastingly, nothing new arising in Him that did not exist before.

Then he gave the reason for this in the most forceful urging toward emigration (hijrah), saying: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death﴾; i.e., they take their souls complete, despite what they have of deficiency in some meanings, because of what they abandoned of the pillar of emigration. This is indicated by the omission of the ta' (in the verb), and in the omission is a guidance that whoever leaves [the duty] while another strives to make it up through charity, pilgrimage, or similar acts of righteousness, it is made up for, because the foundation on which righteous deeds are built is present, namely faith. ﴿Wronging themselves﴾; i.e., by remaining behind from striving (jihad) in the way of Allah, by abandoning emigration, and by staying in the land of war, where they cannot establish all the rites of the religion. ﴿They will say﴾; i.e., the angels, rebuking them: ﴿In what [condition] were you?﴾; i.e., in what matter of deeds and states was your residence in the land of war?

Since the purpose of this question is rebuke for abandoning emigration, ﴿They will say﴾ (p-373), making excuses: ﴿We were oppressed in the earth﴾; i.e., the land of the disbelievers, where we could not establish the religion. It seems they used the general term to indicate that, in their view, because of its vastness and the abundance of disbelievers, it was the whole earth. So it is as if it were said: "Was this excuse accepted from them?" It is said: "No, because they were not weak with respect to emigration." So it is as if [the text] said: "What was said to them?" And it is said: ﴿They [the angels] said﴾; i.e., the angels, making clear that they were not too weak to emigrate to a place where they could be safe in their religion: ﴿Was not the earth of Allah spacious, so that you might emigrate therein?﴾; i.e., the One encompassing all things, to whom all things belong; ﴿spacious﴾, so that, because of its spaciousness, you could go ﴿therein﴾ (ḍāribīna fīhā); i.e., to wherever the obstacle that stands between you and your religion is removed.

Thus the verse contains ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which something is omitted from one part and its counterpart from another, each part indicating the other): the mention of jihad first, in ﴿And Allah has preferred those who strive﴾ (4:95), indicates its omission second, after ﴿wronging themselves﴾; and the mention of emigration second indicates its omission first, through remaining behind from it. For this reason, He singled out the first group with the promise of the best reward.

When they were rebuked for abandoning emigration, their recompense was stated as a consequence, so it is said: ﴿Those, their refuge is Jahannam﴾; i.e., they are far from the good that they sought for themselves, because of their abandonment of the obligatory duty, their increasing the numbers of the disbelievers, and their spreading among the faces of the people (p-374) [i.e., their mixing with them]. ﴿And evil is it as a destination﴾. Al-Bukhari narrated in (the books of) Tafsir and Fitan, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that some people among the Muslims were with the polytheists, increasing the numbers of the polytheists, during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). An arrow would be shot at one of them and would strike and kill him, or he would be struck and killed. Then Allah, the Exalted, revealed: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death﴾.

Since He had threatened those who abandoned emigration (hijrah), He followed that with something that adds to the fear of the one who stays behind, by mentioning those who were not included in the category of those held accountable through capability, in the form of an exception (istithna'), as an alert that they deserve to be treated equally in the ruling, were it not for God's grace upon them. So He said, as an explanation that those excepted from among them are lying in their claim of being oppressed: ﴿Except the oppressed (al-mustad'afin)﴾; that is, those whose weakness was found to be real in fact, and who were counted as weak, and whom others overpowered: ﴿of the men and the women and the children﴾. Then He clarified their weakness by His saying: ﴿who are unable to devise a plan﴾; that is, to carry out the emigration; ﴿nor are they able to find a way﴾; that is, to it.

When the emigration (hijrah) was arduous, some of the strong would abandon it and make weakness an excuse, and sometimes one who was able, under hardship, would think he was not able. So he dispelled this by pointing to them with the demonstrative of distance, saying: ﴿Then those﴾. And since it is for God - glorified and exalted be He - to do whatever He wills, and nothing is obligatory upon Him, nor is anything ugly from Him, rather He may punish the obedient, bless the disobedient, and do and say whatever He wills: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ [al-Anbiya understanding: 23]. He placed these excused ones in the position of hope, to signal that abandoning emigration is of the utmost peril, so He said: ﴿Perhaps God﴾; that is, the hoped-for, the most fitting and worthy of sovereignty, the one encompassing the attributes of perfection: ﴿will pardon them﴾; that is, even had He seized them, it would have been His right. Whatever comes in the Qur'an of this kind is an indication of this meaning. And the saying of Ibn 'Abbas - may God be pleased with both of them -: "Indeed, 'perhaps' (ʿasā) from God is obligatory," means that, although it is His right to do whatever He wills, He does only what wisdom requires, according to what the sound intellect deems right. ﴿And God is﴾; that is, the King to whom belongs everything; so there is no objection to Him, eternally and forever: ﴿Pardoning (ʿafuww)﴾; that is, He erases the sin when He wills, so He does not punish for it, though He may rebuke for it. ﴿Forgiving (ghafur)﴾; that is, He removes its trace entirely, root and branch, such that He neither punishes for it nor rebukes, and it is not mentioned at all. Perhaps pardon (ʿafw) relates to men, and forgiveness (ghufran) to women and children.

When He had warned against abandoning emigration (hijrah), He encouraged it with what would console against the whispering of Satan, that if one were to leave the homeland for ease, he would fall into the severity of estrangement; and that he might perhaps undertake hardship and die before reaching his goal. So He (exalted is He) said: ﴿And whoever emigrates﴾; that is, whoever makes emigration for all that Allah—glorified and exalted is He—and His Messenger ﷺ have commanded him to emigrate for; ﴿in the way of Allah﴾; that is, the way of the One for whom there is no greater dominion, no clearer path, and no wider; ﴿he will find in the earth﴾; that is, in the expanse of its length and breadth; ﴿many a refuge﴾; that is, a place of escape, a direction to go, and a place of movement, which becomes a locus of *muraghamah* (defiance): he angers his enemies by it and rubs their noses in the dust through the ease and good condition that he attains, so that they are humiliated by what they inflicted upon him of ill treatment. From *al-raghm*, which is abasement and humiliation; its root is the sticking of the nose to *al-raghām*, which is dust. You say: "I *raghamtu* so-and-so," meaning: you abandoned him while he disliked your leaving him, due to the humiliation that befalls him thereby.

Since that place, though one, is by its vastness made of many parts, it was described with what implies plurality, so He said ﴿many﴾. Since *muraghamah* is a pleasure of the spirit, and it is more precious than the pleasure of the body, He placed it first; He followed it with His saying ﴿and abundance﴾; that is, in provision, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Fast and you will be healthy; travel and you will gain," related by al-Tabarani from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), and its wording is: "Wage war and emigrate, and you will prosper."

Since the emigrant may die before reaching the Prophet ﷺ, and thus be thought not to have attained the emigration despite having endured leaving his land, He said: ﴿And whoever leaves his house﴾; that is, let alone his land; ﴿emigrating to Allah﴾; that is, the pleasure of the King, to whom belongs all perfection; ﴿and His Messenger﴾; that is, so that he may be with him; ﴿then death overtakes him﴾; that is, after his leaving his house, even if before departing from his land; ﴿his reward has certainly become due﴾; that is, for his emigration—according to the promise, by way of bounty, not by way of what is merited by justice—﴿from Allah﴾; that is, the One who has complete encompassing knowledge, so nothing diminishes Him; and likewise every one who intends good but does not attain it: "There is no envy except in two," so He will fulfill it for him with the fulfillment that the generous among you undertake.

Since some of them may fall short of reaching the goal because of their slackness in their journey, or in leaving their land, and thus he thinks that this emigration of his does not make up for his shortcoming, He said: ﴿And Allah is﴾; that is, the One who possesses all attributes of perfection; ﴿Forgiving﴾; that is, of shortcoming, if there was any; ﴿Merciful﴾; He honors, after forgiveness, with all kinds of honors.

When He made travel obligatory for jihad and hijrah, and travel in general is a source of hardship, how much more so is their travel, combined with what adds to the hardship in them, namely fear of the enemies? He mentioned the lightening of the prayer through shortening (qasr), by His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿And when you travel in the land﴾, meaning: by travelling; ﴿in the land﴾, of whatever kind the travel is, provided it is not for disobedience. Since shortening is a concession (rukhsah) and not an obligation ('azimah), He clarified it by His saying: ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾, meaning: no sin and no inclination, ﴿in shortening﴾. Since shortening applies only to some of the prayers, He used the preposition for this purpose, and to indicate that it concerns the quantity and not the manner, so He said: ﴿of the prayer﴾, meaning: shorten if you wish, and complete if you wish. The Sunnah explained which prayers are shortened, how many rak'ahs are reduced from them, and that the shortening concerns quantity and not the manner, such as by gesturing (ima'), for example in the prayer of fear. This is shown by the saying of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, to Ya'la ibn Umayyah, when he said to him: "How do you shorten while we are secure?": "I wondered at what you wondered at, so I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about that, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'It is a charity which Allah has bestowed upon you, so accept His charity.'" This is the true meaning of shortening, and what the word "min" (from) indicates. As for gesturing and the like among the forms of the prayer of fear, that is a substitution (ibdal), not shortening. The context, as you see, points to the great importance of this matter, and that nothing removes it from the responsible person, and it indicates that exposing oneself to danger with one's life and property does not cancel jihad or hijrah, since fear and danger are the basis of their affair and the aim of their intention. This is the secret of His saying: ﴿if you fear that those who disbelieve will attack you﴾, meaning: will mingle with you in a disturbing way, not that it is a condition for shortening, as the Sunnah has clarified by negating its being a condition. The conclusion is that this condition was mentioned for this purpose, not to imply the opposite of what is stated (mukhalafat al-mafhum li al-manṭuq, i.e., the implied meaning contrary to the explicit meaning), as the Sunnah attests. The prayer before hijrah was two rak'ahs, two rak'ahs, and then it was completed after hijrah, as an indication that Medina is the abode of residence, while what came before it was a place of travel and relocation. Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and Ahmad narrated, and this is his wording, from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The prayer was prescribed as two rak'ahs, two rak'ahs. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ arrived in Medina, the prayer of travel was confirmed, and it was increased in the prayer of residence."

When He mentioned fear from them, He gave the reason, indicating by using the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, and by the active participle, that whoever is involved in disbelief even for a moment, is deeply immersed in it; or that the one who is naturally inclined to enmity, indicated by the word "kawn" (were), is in fact the one firmly established in disbelief, whose death in that state is decreed. So He said: ﴿Indeed, the disbelievers﴾, meaning: those among them who are firmly established in disbelief; ﴿have been﴾, meaning: by nature and disposition; perhaps He indicated that they are the defeated ones by His saying ﴿to you﴾ rather than ﴿against you﴾; ﴿an enemy﴾. Since "enemy" is a word that applies equally to the singular and the plural, He said: ﴿clear﴾, meaning: manifest in enmity, attacking you intending harm whenever they find a way to do so. Perhaps they find an opportunity in the length of the prayer, so for this reason I have shortened it. Had it not been that there is no concession for it in any way, I would have removed it from you in such a situation, or I would have made the lightening in the time, so that I commanded delay. But the souls have no purification without performing it at the time I have set, and other requirements.

(p-٣٨٠) When He, glory be to Him and exalted, had completed the explanation of shortening the prayer in its number, combined with fear for what was mentioned, and since the presence of the Prophet ﷺ was a sign of safety, through being supported by the angels, the promise of protection from people, his well-known bravery, the terror (of the enemy) that he was given victory with, and other matters indicating that the final outcome belongs to him, He, glory be to Him and exalted, explained the manner of the prayer in fear. He showed that the prayer of fear is performed when one is in the company of his presence just as it is performed when one feels lonely in his absence, ﷺ. So its permissibility for a group among whom he ﷺ is not present is understood by implication of agreement (mafhūm muwāfaqah). He, glory be to Him and exalted, said: ﴿And when you are among them﴾, in the state of fear whose obligation has been mentioned earlier, ﴿among them﴾, i.e., among your companions, whether that is while traveling or while at home. ﴿And you establish for them the prayer﴾, i.e., you begin and bring it into being for them, ﴿the prayer﴾, i.e., the complete one, which is the obligatory one. ﴿Then let one group of them stand with you﴾, i.e., in the prayer. ﴿And let the other group stand facing the enemy﴾, and they patrol every place from which the enemy could come. ﴿And let them take﴾, i.e., those who pray, because they are the ones in need of this matter, since their entering a state in which laying down weapons is more fitting, ﴿their weapons﴾, just as one who is outside the prayer takes them. The reason for the command concerning the prayer of fear, as in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim and others, from Jābir, may Allah (Exalted) be pleased with him, is that: "They fought alongside the Prophet ﷺ, and they fought a group from Juhaynah, and they fought a severe battle. Jābir, may Allah (Exalted) be pleased with him, said: 'When we had prayed the noon prayer, the polytheists said: If we had attacked them at one moment, we would have cut them off.'

(p-٣٨١) Then Jibrīl, upon him be prayer and peace, informed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of that, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ told us about it. He said: And they said: Indeed, a prayer is coming to them that is more beloved to them than their children. When the afternoon prayer came, we arranged ourselves in two rows, and the polytheists were between us and the qiblah...," the hadith. ﴿Then when they prostrate﴾ may mean the prostration in its apparent sense, so the pronoun in ﴿then let them be﴾ refers to the group, those among whom this group is, mentioned by way of the pronoun in His saying "And when you are among them" and in "let one group of them stand", i.e., when those who stood with you in the prayer prostrate, then let those spoken of, namely the others, those among whom you are and this group is part of them, be ﴿behind you﴾. So when this group has completed its prayer, let it go to guard duty. ﴿And let another group come﴾, i.e., from the congregation, ﴿who have not prayed, and let them pray with you﴾, just as the first group prayed. If the prayer is two units and each group has not prayed the entire prayer, then you should give the salam with the second group. If it is four units and each party has not prayed the entire prayer, then you should complete your prayer, and let it go to face the enemy, and let another group come, and so on until the prayer is complete. It is also possible that the intended meaning of prostration is the prayer, by the usage of naming a part for the whole. So it is as if He said: "When they pray", i.e., complete their prayer, as the allusion previously indicated. The pronoun in "then let them be" (p-٣٨٢) at that point refers to the group that prostrated. His saying ﴿and let them take﴾ may have its pronoun refer to all, lest it be assumed that the command to this applies only to the one praying, since others have no obstacle to taking (weapons) whenever they wish. Or: let all the groups, the guards and those praying, take ﴿their precaution and their weapons﴾ during their prayer, their guarding, their coming to the prayer, and their leaving it. He made caution, which is vigilance and guarding oneself by turning the mind toward what prevents the enemy's scheming, like a tangible instrument. It was specified in its use in the prayer in regard to the enemy. The end of the prayer was specified with additional caution, indicating that the enemy at the beginning of the prayer rarely notice that they are in prayer, unlike at the end. Therefore it was specified with greater caution. This statement, despite its brevity, as you see, admits of all the forms mentioned in jurisprudence (fiqh) for the prayer of fear when the enemy is not in the direction of the qiblah. Moreover, it admits of being applied to the case where the enemy is in the direction of the qiblah, by understanding "behind you" as what the prostration shields you from, and "the coming of the other group" as turning to follow the imam in his actions, and "they have not prayed" meaning: with the condition of following him in them. And Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, is the Guide.

How excellent is the connection of this to the first verses on jihad in this surah: ﴿O you who have believed, take your precaution﴾ [An-Nisa: 71]. This is the returning of the conclusion to the opening. Then He gave the reason for His command in this manner, upon this caution and resolve, by saying, strengthening their encouragement toward that, by directing the address to them (p-٣٨٣): ﴿Those who disbelieved wish﴾, i.e., they desired a great desire; ﴿those who disbelieved﴾, i.e., they engaged in disbelief at some time, so how about one who is drowning in it? ﴿If you were to be unaware﴾, i.e., there occurs for you a heedlessness at some time, ﴿of your weapons﴾. And since strength through instruments is frightening to the enemy and disabling, He said: ﴿and your belongings﴾. And since heedlessness is a clear weakness, His saying ﴿and they would turn upon you﴾ followed from it. He indicated elevation and dominance by His saying ﴿upon you﴾, and indicated swiftness of seizing by His saying ﴿in one turn﴾, and emphasized it by His saying ﴿one﴾.

Since Allah, to whom belongs the favor, had lifted hardship from this Ummah, and rain and illness were burdensome, He said: ﴿There is no blame upon you﴾, i.e., no hardship, ﴿if there is harm to you﴾, i.e., even if it is slight, ﴿from rain﴾, because carrying weapons at that time would cause them to get wet, ﴿or if you are ill﴾, i.e., characterized by illness. The expression by way of description seems to indicate that even the slightest of it does not grant a concession, ﴿to lay down your weapons﴾, because carrying them increases the weakness of the sick.

Since He lightened what He had first obligated regarding taking up weapons by lifting blame in the case of excuse, so the meaning becomes: "Lay them down if you wish", He joined to it, in the form of a command, indicating the obligation of caution against them in every state, His saying ﴿and take your precaution﴾, i.e., in every state, for that is a benefit from which no harm is expected. Then He gave the reason for that by what He gave good news of victory in, as encouragement for the believers and as informing them that the command to resolve is only for (p-٣٨٤) acting upon what He laid down of wisdom in His saying. He linked causes to means, so this is from the category of "Tie it and rely upon Allah." So He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, the one whose knowledge and power encompass all, ﴿has prepared﴾, i.e., from eternity, ﴿for the disbelievers﴾, i.e., those who persist in disbelief, not whoever was characterized by it at some time and then repented from it, ﴿a humiliating punishment﴾, i.e., one that humiliates them by it. Among the greatest of it is your caution, which leaves them no advance against you, and gives them no opportunity against you with it.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 4, verse 103:**

When He taught them what to do in the prayer during fear, He followed that with what they should do after it, lest it be thought that the prayer replaces mere remembrance (dhikr). So He said, pointing to its sequence with it: ﴿So when you have completed the prayer﴾; that is, when you have finished performing it and carried it out in a state of fear or otherwise. ﴿Then remember Allah﴾; that is, by means other than the prayer, because He encompasses everything, and so He deserves to be watched and not forgotten. ﴿standing, sitting, and lying on your sides﴾; that is, in every state. His remembrance is your fortress in every state, against every enemy, whether apparent or hidden.

Since remembrance is the greatest guardian of the servant, a protector against the devils of mankind and jinn, and a calmer of hearts, ﴿Surely in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest﴾ [al-Ra'd: 28], He indicated (p-385) this by commanding the prayer in a state of tranquillity (ṭumaʾnīnah). This draws attention to the great status of the prayer and clarifies that it is the most secure handhold of the religion, its strongest pillar, the most effective polisher of hearts (mujlliyāt al-qulūb) and refiner of souls (muhadhdhibāt al-nufūs), because it comprises the sum of remembrance. ﴿Indeed, the prayer restrains from immorality and wrongdoing, and the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 45]. So He said: ﴿And when you are secure﴾; that is, from what you were facing of fear; ﴿then establish the prayer﴾; that is, perform it with all its features complete, in the same manner you used to perform it before the fear. Then He gave the reason for commanding it in both security and fear, in ease and hardship, while traveling or at home, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, the prayer﴾; He expressed it explicitly where the original form would have been a pronoun, to draw attention to its great status, through the connection it gives the servant to his Worshipped One. ﴿Has been decreed upon the believers as a decree of specified times﴾; that is, it is, although obligatory, a fixed obligation upon Allah's servants in a manner that nothing else shares with it. ﴿Specified times (mawqūtan)﴾; that is, although it is limited, it is bound to well-known times, so it is not permissible to delay it beyond them, whether in security or in fear of missing it. This is what the root *w-q-t* (waqt, "time") indicates: for bodies, through the provisions it causes; and for hearts, through the knowledge and lights it brings.

And since it has become known from this that the verses on jihad in this surah teach caution against harm, and guide toward perfecting stratagems for escaping danger, and that this may lead to following the self and overdoing it, while it also may lead to slackness in the matter of jihad, He followed that with His saying (exalted is He), alerting to earnestness in the matter and that He has left nothing in the prayer (ṣalāh) or otherwise that would distract from it, coordinating with a phrase like: "So do what I have commanded you," or with: ﴿So establish the prayer﴾ [an-Nisa: 103]: ﴿And do not weaken﴾, that is, do not become feeble, and do not slacken by occupying yourselves with remembrance or prayer, for He has made that easy for you, an ease that does not hinder you from anything in the matter of jihad. ﴿In pursuing the people﴾, that is, seeking them with diligence, even if they are at the height of strength and of managing affairs. Then He gave the reason for that in His saying: ﴿If you suffer﴾, that is, pain and hardship arise for you in jihad, from being killed and what is less than that; ﴿then indeed they suffer as you suffer﴾, that is, because what befalls you from that befalls them too. So they should not be more patient in their falsehood than you are in your truth.

When He had made clear what would prevent them from weakness, which is common to both sides, He explained what impels them to advance, since it is specific to them. So He said: ﴿And you hope﴾, that is, you, ﴿from Allah﴾, that is, the One to whom belong all the Most Beautiful Names and the Highest Attributes, ﴿what they do not hope﴾, that is, of victory, honor, generosity, and kindness, because you fight for Him while they fight for Shaytan. This applies to everyone who enjoins what is good and forbids what is evil, whether that is in fighting the disbelievers or not.

And since knowledge is the foundation of all good, and wisdom, which is the culmination of knowledge and the utmost of power, is the gathering of the Highest Attributes, He (exalted is He) said: ﴿And Allah is﴾, that is, the One who commands you with these commands, the One who encompasses everything: ﴿Knowing﴾, that is, of perfect knowledge; so He commands only what is of perfect goodness, beneficial for the religion and the world; ﴿Wise﴾, so He perfects the circumstances for the one He commands, and guides him in speech and deed. Whoever He knows to have good in him, He wills it for him and raises him in the ranks of happiness; and whoever He knows to have evil in him, He schemes against him, and overturns his beginning and his end.

(p-390) And He follows that with His saying: ﴿And seek forgiveness from God﴾; that is, He to whom belongs complete encompassing (of all things) and absolute self-sufficiency. ﴿He has always been﴾; that is, eternally, without beginning and without end, ﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾. This seeking of forgiveness is not for a sin, since he is exalted above that and protected from it, but it is for a lofty and perfect station, in order to ascend to something higher and more complete than it. At-Tirmidhi related the occasion of revelation of these verses, up to His saying (may He be exalted): ﴿Then he has certainly strayed into far error﴾ [An-Nisa: 116], in a comprehensive account that explains it fully and sufficiently. He named the Banu Ubayriq as "Bishr," "Bushayr," and "Mubashshir," and did not mention Tu'ma. And God (glory be to Him, exalted) knows best. He said, on the authority of Qatada ibn an-Nu'man, who said:

"There was a household among us called the Banu Ubayriq: Bishr, Bushayr, and Mubashshir. Bushayr was a hypocrite man who composed poetry satirizing the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), then attributed it to some of the Arabs, saying, 'So-and-so said such-and-such.' When the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) heard that poetry, they would say, 'By God, no one composes this poetry except this wicked man.' They were a household in need and poverty, in the Jahiliyyah and in Islam. Then a caravan came from Syria, and my paternal uncle Rifa'a ibn Zayd bought a load of dirmak (fine white flour) and placed it in an upper storeroom of his, in which there was weaponry: a coat of mail and a sword. Someone broke in from beneath the house, the storeroom was breached, and the food and weapons were taken. When morning came, my uncle Rifa'a came to me and said: 'O nephew, we have been attacked during this night; our storeroom was breached, and our food and weapons were taken.' He said: 'We searched the house, and it was said to us: We saw the Banu Ubayriq kindle a fire this night, and we think nothing except that it was on some of your food.'" He said: "The Banu Ubayriq had said, while we were asking around the house: 'By God, we do not think your companion (the thief) is anyone but Labid ibn Sahl, a man among us who is righteous and Muslim.' When Labid heard this, he drew his sword and said: 'Am I a thief?! By God, this sword will certainly come upon you, or you will make this theft clear!' They said: 'Keep away from us, O man, for you are not its perpetrator.' We kept searching the house until we had no doubt that they were its perpetrators. My uncle said to me: 'O nephew, if you went to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him...' Qatada said: 'So I went to him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I will consider the matter."' When the Banu Ubayriq heard, they came to a man among them called Usayr ibn Urwa, and spoke to him about it. A group of people from the household gathered over this and said: 'O Messenger of God, Qatada ibn an-Nu'man and his uncle have targeted a household among us, a household of Islam and righteousness, accusing them of theft without evidence or certainty.' Qatada said: 'I came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and spoke with him, and he said: "You have targeted a household of whom Islam and righteousness were mentioned, accusing them of theft without certainty and proof?!"' He said: 'My uncle said to me: "O nephew, what have you done?" So I informed him of what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had said to me, and he said: "God is the One sought for help."' Then the Qur'an was soon revealed: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth﴾ [An-Nisa: 105] up to: ﴿an advocate﴾ [An-Nisa: 105], concerning the Banu Ubayriq; ﴿And seek forgiveness from God﴾ for what you said to Qatada; ﴿Indeed, God is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾; up to His saying: ﴿Then We will give him a great reward﴾ [An-Nisa: 114]. When the Qur'an was revealed, the weapons were brought to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he returned them to Rifa'a. When the Qur'an was revealed, Bushayr joined the polytheists, and he settled with Sulafa bint Sa'd ibn Sumayya. Then God (glory be to Him, exalted) revealed: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger﴾ [An-Nisa: 115], up to His saying: ﴿far error﴾ [An-Nisa: 116]."

Ibn Ishaq related the hadith in as-Sira and added: "Hassan composed some verses while he was staying with her, so she drove him away, and he went to at-Ta'if. He entered a house to steal from it, and fell upon it and died." Quraysh then said: "By God, no companion of Muhammad who has any good in him ever leaves him."

(p-393) When He forbade him from disputing on behalf of the treacherous in general, that is, whoever has committed some treachery, He followed it with a prohibition on arguing for those who deliberately commit treachery. Glorified and exalted is He, He said: ﴿And do not dispute﴾, meaning at any time, ﴿on behalf of those who betray﴾, meaning those from whom deliberate betrayal recurs, ﴿themselves﴾, by bringing themselves to ruin through disobedience concerning the hidden matters entrusted to them. The use of the plural, although the verse was revealed concerning one man, is for generality and to threaten whoever helped him from among his people. It is also possible that the verbal pattern *ifti'al* (the eighth verbal form, *iftaʿala*) indicates that betrayal does not occur except repeatedly, for a person first resolves upon it and then carries it out. So the least of it is that he has betrayed himself twice. The Imam said, in substance, that the threat in this verse is very great, because He, glorified and exalted, rebuked the best of creation in His sight and the most honoured of them before Him with this rebuke, and he did nothing but what was right outwardly. How then will it be with one who knows the inner reality and assists the people of falsehood? And how much more so if it is with others? Then, glorified and exalted is He, indicated that whoever betrays another is exaggerating in betrayal, through the resolve and the betrayal of another, which entails the betrayal of himself. Therefore the verse was concluded with the causal explanation in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, meaning the Majestic, the Great, Possessor of majesty and honour, ﴿does not love﴾, meaning does not honour, ﴿those who are (p-394) habitual betrayers, sinners﴾, in two intensive forms, since the degrees of those who exaggerate in betrayal vary. Along with this there is an appeal to the sympathy of whoever committed betrayal only once. Glorified and exalted is He placed this first, because in it there is a removal of harm from the innocent and the bringing of benefit to him.

Then he followed it with a censure of this traitor, of his lack of reflection, and of the notice that arguing on his behalf is of little benefit. So He - glory be to Him, and exalted - said, marvelling at them, in a manner that serves as a rationale for what precedes it: ﴿They hide from the people﴾; that is, these traitors: Ṭu'mah and whoever backs him, while he knows the inner truth of the matter; ﴿from the people﴾, out of shame before them and fear that they might harm them, because of seeing them, standing with the illusion, like cattle; ﴿but they do not hide from Allah﴾; that is, they do not seek or achieve concealment by refraining from treachery, from Allah, the One than whom nothing is more manifest, by virtue of His attributes of perfection; ﴿while He is with them﴾; that is, while the state is that He is with them, nothing of their conditions escapes Him, and nothing of their punishment is beyond His power. So concealment from Him is only possible by abandoning treachery and by pure sincerity. Woe to them for the most prevalent of their deeds, sayings and states! ﴿When﴾; that is, at the time when; ﴿they plot﴾; that is, they arrange at night, by way of deep reflection and perfecting the opinion; ﴿what He does not approve of in speech﴾; that is, of deceit and swearing to it. So they feel no shame before Him and do not fear, because ignorance and heedlessness have taken hold of their hearts, and because of their lack of faith in the Unseen. (p-395) When He had established His knowledge - glory be to Him, and exalted - of this from their state, He generalised, saying: ﴿And Allah is ever﴾; that is, the One in whose grip everything is, because He is the One who has no equal; ﴿of what they do﴾; that is, of this and other than this; ﴿encompassing﴾; that is, in knowledge and power.

When He, glory be to Him and exalted, had rebuked them for their ignorance, He warned against supporting them. He said, making clear that such support would not benefit them at all, and frightening them intensely by addressing them directly with this admonition and address, and then with a demonstrative pointing at them: ﴿Here you are, you people﴾. He increased the warning by specifying the matter with what is of disputation, which is the most intense hostility, taken from "jadl al-habl" (the tight twisting of a rope), which refers to the intensity of its twisting, and by expressing it in the form of mufa'ala (the third verbal form, denoting mutual action), so He said, clarifying that what is intended by the preceding sentence is a threat: ﴿you argued on their behalf﴾, in this incident or in others, ﴿in the life of this world﴾, that is, by means of the causes that were made available to you.

When He had warned them, He rebuked them for their lack of insight, and, as an increase in the warning, that their disputing on their behalf is a cause for a judgment being brought before Him, glory be to Him and exalted, He said: ﴿Then who will dispute with God﴾, that is, the One to whom all majesty belongs, ﴿on their behalf﴾, that is, when the causes are cut off, ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾. The situation does not differ in this regard whether the "ha" in "ha antum" (Here you are) is for alerting, or is a substitute for the interrogative hamza (the hamzat istifham, the question particle), as previously stated, for the sense of disapproval here is clear in both cases.

Since among the greatest of excellences is a person's restraint from what he has no knowledge of, He linked to the sentence from its beginning, without restricting it to the Day of Resurrection, and as an alert to the ugliness of disputing on their behalf, given the limitation of the knowledge of creatures, His saying: ﴿Or who will be a guardian over them﴾, that is, in what comes of time, ﴿a guardian﴾. That is, one who knows of them what God, glory be to Him and exalted, knows, by counting their deeds so that nothing of them escapes him, in order to dispute with God on their behalf, so that what they have departed from is established for them, what they have not engaged in is negated from them, and so that he may watch over and protect them from the harm and distress that fate brings upon them.

When He forbade supporting the betrayer and warned against it, He exhorted [the people] to repent of every evil. He said, conjoining it to what is implicitly understood, "So whoever persists in this kind of disputing will find Allah All-Knowing, All-Wise," and [then]: ﴿And whoever does wrong﴾; that is, an ugly deed, transgressive, harming another in the sight of the Law, intentionally, as Ṭu'mah did, or unintentionally; ﴿or wrongs himself﴾ by something that does not extend to others, whether it is shirk or other than shirk, or by being content with a thing whose lower value he accepts for himself. He did not call it "evil" (sū') because he does not intend to harm himself in what harms him in the present [life]. ﴿Then seeks forgiveness from Allah﴾; that is, asks the Supreme King for His forgiveness through repentance, with its conditions; ﴿will find Allah﴾; that is, the One who combines every perfection; ﴿Forgiving﴾; that is, effacing the lapses; (p-397) ﴿Merciful﴾; that is, exceedingly generous toward whoever turns to Him. [The Prophet (ﷺ)] said: "Whoever draws near to Me a span, I draw near to him a cubit; whoever draws near to Me a cubit, I draw near to him a fathom; and whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him running." 

Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh narrated from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, and Abū Yaʿlā al-Mawṣilī narrated from Abū al-Dardāʾ, may Allah be pleased with him, that this verse abrogated (naskh, i.e., the annulment of a earlier ruling by a later revelation) ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 123], and that it was revealed after it.

When he (Allah) had urged repentance and encouraged it, He made clear that the harm of a person's sin does not extend beyond himself, as an incitement to repentance and a stirring towards it, because every person is naturally disposed to love benefit for himself and to repel harm from himself. So He said: ﴿And whoever earns a sin﴾ — whatever sin it may be — ﴿then he earns it only against himself﴾, because its evil returns upon him, since Allah is ever watchful over him (lit. "lies in wait for him") and will surely requite him for it, without doubt, not bearing any part of his sin upon another, just as he does not bear any part of another's sin upon himself. And "al-kasb" (earning, acquisition) means doing what brings benefit or repels harm.

Since this cannot happen except with knowledge and wisdom, He (Exalted) said: ﴿And Allah is ever﴾ — that is, the One who possesses perfect comprehensiveness, eternally and everlastingly — ﴿All-Knowing﴾ — that is, of perfect knowledge of its minutest and greatest details, so He leaves nothing of it out — ﴿All-Wise﴾, so He does not requite except in proportion to the sin, and when He wills something He places it in its most fitting place, so none other than Him can undo any part of it.

(p-398) When He mentioned what pertains to a person's own sin, He followed it with what extends its harm to others, saying: ﴿And whoever earns a fault﴾ — that is, a sin he did not commit deliberately — ﴿or a sin﴾ — that is, a sin he committed deliberately. Since slander (buhtan) is extremely grave, few dare to commit it, so He indicated it with the particle of delay (thumma), saying: ﴿then throws it upon an innocent one﴾ — that is, he attributes it to someone who did not do it, as Ṭu'mah did regarding the Jew, and Ibn Ubayy regarding the truthful one (al-Ṣiddiqah), may Allah (Exalted) be pleased with her. He magnified the crime of the one who does this by the form of the verb (ifti'al) in His saying: ﴿then he has borne﴾, and by His saying: ﴿a slander (buhtanan)﴾ — that is, a false accusation (khaṭar kadhib) that stuns the one it is aimed at because of its enormity. It seems to be an indication of the blame that befalls the slanderer in this world. ﴿And a manifest sin (ithman mubinan)﴾ — that is, a great sin, for which he will be punished in the Hereafter. It was manifest because he knows the betrayal of his own soul and the innocence of the one accused; and because Allah, glorified and exalted, has made it His beautiful custom to reveal the innocence of the one falsely accused, one day, by some means, even if only to some of the people.

When He - glorified and exalted - had admonished, warned, forbidden and commanded in this incident, He showed His favour to His Prophet ﷺ in preserving him from what they wanted of him, namely arguing on behalf of the traitor, by His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Had it not been for the grace of God﴾, that is, the Sovereign, the Most High (p-399) ﴿upon you﴾, that is, by sending down the Book; ﴿and His mercy﴾, that is, by exalting your affair and preserving you from every schemer, and by protecting you in your companions, who came to dispute on behalf of their cousin, the thief of the coat of mail, by holding to the apparent and by not intending obstinacy. ﴿A party of them would have resolved﴾, that is, a group among them who had the capacity for turning and scheming, who constantly devise opinions, turn matters over and revolve ideas in arranging what they want, ﴿to lead you astray﴾, that is, to bring you into that by ruling for the innocence of Ṭu'ma, ﴿but God protected you in your companions, so they did not resolve upon that; they only intended to defend their companion with what they had not verified. Had they resolved upon it, they would not have led you astray.﴾ ﴿Yet they lead none astray﴾, that is, in any state of this resolve, ﴿except themselves﴾, since the burden of that falls upon them. ﴿And they do not harm you﴾, that is, they do not bring harm to you, in present or in wealth, by misguidance or otherwise, ﴿in any way﴾. This is a promise of the continuance of preservation, outwardly and inwardly, like the verse of al-Ma'ida as well, although this one, by its context, is evident in the inward and that one is evident in the outward. ﴿And God has sent down upon you﴾, that is, He to whom belongs all greatness, ﴿upon you﴾, and you are the greatest of creation in preserving your community, ﴿the Book﴾, that is, the one whose perfection and its combining of the two good abodes was indicated at the beginning of the narrative, ﴿and the wisdom﴾ (p-400), that is, understanding of all the aims of the Book, so that your actions and the actions of those who follow you in it are in the most perfect conditions, and you attain the realisation of knowledge and the mastery of action. He generalised with His saying: ﴿and taught you what you did not know﴾, that is, of the difficult matters and others, the unseen and the witnessed, concerning the affairs of the religion and of the world. ﴿And the grace of God upon you has been immense﴾, that is, He who is singular in every perfection, ﴿immense﴾, that is, beyond this, of matters that do not fall under enumeration. This is among the greatest proofs that knowledge is the most noble of virtues.

The people of Ṭu'ma had conferred with the Prophet (ﷺ) about defending him; so Allah, glorified is He, alerted them and others to what should be the subject of private consultation (tanājī), and wherein good counsel and mutual consultation are fitting, in a manner that forbids anything else most strongly, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk﴾; that is, the secret talk of all who confer privately; ﴿except for one who orders charity﴾; that is, the secret talk of one who does so; and since He specified charity because wealth was scarce in that situation, He generalized by saying: ﴿or what is right﴾; that is, whatever right it is, of what the Law permits, of charity or otherwise.

And since reconciliation between people (iṣlāḥ dhāt al-bayn) is a weighty matter, He drew attention to its greatness by singling it out, saying: ﴿or reconciliation between people﴾; that is, in general. Thus Allah, glorified and exalted is He, made clear that whatever is not excluded from private consultation contains no good; and whatever has no good in it is to be avoided. This is as Aḥmad and al-Ṭabarānī in al-Kabīr related with a chain of narration that is acceptable (lā ba's bihi), and this is the wording of the latter, from Ibn 'Abbās (may Allah be pleased with them both), from the Prophet (ﷺ), that ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) said: "Matters are three: a matter whose rightness has been made clear to you, so follow it; a matter whose error has been made clear to you, so avoid it; and a matter about which there is disagreement, so refer it to its knowing scholar."

Since the implied sense is: "Whoever orders something of that kind, his secret talk is good, and he has a reward for it," He followed it with His saying: ﴿And whoever does that﴾; that is, the great matter which he was commanded of these things; ﴿seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾; who possesses the attributes of perfection; because an action has no spirit except through intention (niyya); ﴿then We shall give him﴾; that is, in the Hereafter; by a promise that does not fail; ﴿a great reward﴾. This verse is among the greatest proofs that what is required of outward acts is the care of the states of the heart in sincerity of intention, and the purifying of the motive from turning toward a worldly aim; so if it is for show (riyāʾ), it is reversed and becomes among the greatest corruptions.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 4, verse 115:

When He, glorified and exalted is He, had arranged the great reward for conformity, He arranged the severe punishment for opposition and defiance (al-mushaqqah), and He left the opponent to himself, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger﴾; that is, the perfect one in messengerhood (al-Rusuliyyah), so that he is in his heart, or in some part of his action, in a direction other than his direction, in the manner of overpowering (al-muqahara). He expressed it with the imperfect verb, out of His mercy, glorified is He, by restricting the threat to continuity; and He made the qaf clear (idhhar), as an indication that it is tied to open defiance (al-mujahara). And because the context concerns the people of idols, and they are open defiers, and he who stole the two coats of mail, whose case was the cause of the revelation of the verse, openly defied at the end of his story, as has passed.

And since it is in the context of teaching the Sharia, which was not known before its revelation, and not in the context of a religion known by reason, He brought "min" (from), to restrict the threat to what comes after the announcement of that; so He said: ﴿after what﴾; and if it were omitted, the restriction of the threat would be understood to apply only to one who spent the whole period of absence in opposition. And since what the Prophet ﷺ brought was in the utmost clarity, He said: ﴿has become clear to him the guidance﴾; that is, the proof, which is its cause. And since one who opposes the consensus (ijma') does not become a disbeliever except by rejecting what is known necessarily (al-ma'lum bil-darurah), He expressed after the clarification by "following," so He said: ﴿and follows other than the way﴾; that is, the path of; ﴿the believers﴾; that is, those for whom faith has become a firmly established quality. The intended meaning is the figurative path (al-tariq al-ma'nawi): the aspect of resemblance is the bodily movement that leads to the goal in the sensible realm, and the psychic movement in the preliminaries of the proof that leads to the goal in the intelligible realm. ﴿We shall leave him﴾; that is, with Our authority in this world and the Hereafter; ﴿to what he has turned to﴾; that is, We shall leave him to what he chose for himself, and treated his original nature (fitrah) by it, as abandonment from Us toward him; ﴿and We shall burn him﴾; that is, in the Hereafter; ﴿in Hell﴾; that is, he will meet it with aversion, harshness, and scowling, just as he scowled at Our allies and opposed them.

And since the implied meaning is: "so he is certainly going to it," He explained its condition in that, so He said: ﴿and evil it is as a destination﴾. This verse indicates that consensus is a proof (hujjah), because one is threatened only for opposing the truth. Likewise the hadith: «"A group of my nation will not cease to be standing upon the command of Allah" - and in another narration: "dominant upon the truth" - "until the command of Allah comes."» It was related from the Prophet ﷺ by the Companions - may Allah be pleased with them - Thawban, al-Mughirah, Jabir ibn Samurah, Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, Mu'awiyah, Anas, and Abu Hurayrah; some of their hadiths are in the Two Sahihs, some in the Sunan, some in the Musnads, some in the Mu'jams, and others. The basis of the proof is that the group to which the Prophet ﷺ testified as being upon the truth is among the people of consensus. And Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is the Granter of success.

Since the one who does this, after the guidance has been made clear, is the People of the Book and those among the hypocrites whom they misled, by the doubts they cast upon them, and so turned them back into the darkness of polytheism and doubt, after the rays of monotheism had dazzled their eyes, the mention of it has been made fitting. Allah, glorified and exalted be He, states the reason, to honour the people of Islam, to urge adherence to their guidance, to censure those who oppose them, and to threaten such people. This is an indication that whoever breaks the consensus (ijma') of the Muslims has the ruling of the polytheists, so how much more so is the one who opposes the messengers. ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, that is, the One, the Absolute, for there is no equal to Him, ﴿does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾, that is, that association (shirk) should occur with Him, by any person and with any thing, because whoever disparages the King deserves perdition and destruction, and the thief of a coat of mail is the most deserving of people of that. ﴿But He forgives what is less than that﴾, that is, everything else, ﴿that is less than that﴾, that is, the matter that leaves no room for abhorrence (p-404), as is the case with one who has submitted to peace, entered the bond of servitude, and then desire overcame him so that he fell short in some kinds of service. Then He indicates the implementation of His command by His saying: ﴿for whomever He wills﴾.

Since the implied sense is: "For whoever associates partners with Him has indeed fabricated a grave sin," He joined to it His saying: ﴿And whoever associates partners with Allah﴾, that is, commits this utterly foul act, at any time, whether in the past, the present, or the future, persisting in renewing it, ﴿with Allah﴾, that is, the King whose sole greatness no one disputes, for there is no concealment of that from anyone. ﴿Has indeed strayed﴾, that is, has gone away from the path that leads to the goal, ﴿a far straying﴾, from which the safety of its perpetrator is not possible. He omitted the premise of fabrication, which is the deliberate intent to lie, and mentioned the premise of straying, because the bulk of the context concerns the Arabs, the people of idols, among whom ignorance was widespread, unlike what preceded regarding the People of the Book, for their disbelief was with knowledge, and so it was a deliberate lie.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 4, verse 117:**

Since the hypocrites were the primary target of these verses, and most of them were idol-worshippers, the statement fits perfectly with his words, explaining that associating partners with God is misguidance: ﴿in﴾, meaning "what"; ﴿yad'una﴾ ("they call upon"). How apt it is that the worship of idols is described as calling upon them, indicating that any object of worship that cannot be called upon in times of need to hear and respond is, for its worshipper, the most ignorant of the ignorant. Since everything other than Him, glorified and exalted is He, is beneath Him because it is under His dominion, He said, belittling what they worshipped: ﴿min dunihi﴾, meaning "other than Him," that is, the Most Merciful. Since their objects of worship were many idols, and every multiplicity entails division, need, and weakness, and since they named some of them with female names, such as al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and said of all of them that they were the daughters of God, and said of every idol, "the female of such-and-such a clan," He said: ﴿illa inathan﴾, meaning they made themselves worshippers of females, while they disdain to have daughters themselves. In the tafsir (exegesis) of al-Bukhari it is stated regarding ﴿inathan﴾ that it means lifeless things: stones, clods of earth, or whatever is similar to that. Furthermore, the root *أنث* (\*anatha\*) and the root *وثن* (\*wathana\*) inherently entail multiplicity, softness, and division, all of which are far removed from the rank of divinity. Its full explanation will come, God willing (Exalted is He), in surah al-'Ankabut. This restriction (*qasr*) is a reversal of restriction (*qalb qasr*), since they believed these were gods.
